lines.en: This idea that busy equals productive,
we find it in our lives
and we find it in our jobs,
and we find it in management.
When you have so many things going on,
obviously ideally you're going to try
to get rid of that busyness
and just get right into productivity immediately.
But I found with kids in particular,
the heartfelt moments matter the most, right?
It's not playing soccer mom that matters,
it's the real conversations,
and you see those, even if it's a 2-minute moment,
it becomes so much more impactful
that you start to say,
man, I have got to not
just be busy with these kids.
I have to find ways to connect with them,
because that's what actually creates relationships.
When I then look at work, it's like,
do I need seven meetings?
I don't need that.
I've got to get right
to the heart of this issue.

lessons.speaker: Gabe Larsen
lessons.title: "I'm Growing People, You're Growing Revenue"
lessons.title_ja: 私は人を、あなたは売上を育てる

vocab.ja: 生きるか死ぬか（の重大事）
かかっているもの・重み

quiz.q: How does the speaker compare the stakes at work and with kids?
choices: The stakes with kids can be life and death.
Kids are less important than revenue.
quiz.explain: He says some things with kids are life and death, so the stakes are different from his job.

quiz.q: What did his wife do at some point?
choices: She moved to a new city.
quiz.explain: He says she ended up quitting her career.

quiz.q: What does "a whole basketball team" mean here?
choices: His kids play basketball every day.
quiz.explain: It's a joke: they have enough kids to make a basketball team.

quiz.q: What did the speaker use to say to his wife?
choices: She should go back to work.
Staying with the kids all day must be hard and boring.
quiz.explain: He said it must be so hard and boring to be with the kids all day.

quiz.q: What was his wife's answer?
choices: She agreed her life was boring.
She was growing people while he was only growing revenue.
She wanted him to stay home.
She wanted to grow the company's revenue.
quiz.explain: She said she grows and shapes humans, and his life of growing revenue is the boring one.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: With kids, there are some things
that are in fact life and death.
And then you put
that in just perspective with your job,
and certainly want to do well,
but the stakes are a little bit different
than they are when you're talking
about like your tiny human beings.
I've talked to my wife about that.
At some point, you know,
she ended up quitting her career,
now that we have a whole basketball team.
For a while there, I remember saying to her,
"Oh man, it must be so hard.
It's so boring, you know, these kids.
You got to be with all these punks all day."
And I remember one time she
looked at me and she's like,
"You know, I'm growing people every day,
and you're growing revenue.
What a boring life you have, you know?
I'm like growing these humans and shaping them."
The emotional centeredness definitely gets
a little bit different, I think,
as you move down this path.

lessons.speaker: Sam Yagan
lessons.title: Bringing the Founder Mentality to Parenting
lessons.title_ja: 創業者の考え方を子育てに

vocab.ja: ガードレール・守るべき枠

quiz.q: Which pair of qualities does the speaker say is key to his success?
quiz.explain: He is optimistic and believes in what he sells, but also knows you must execute and deliver.

quiz.q: How does he feel about his kids' abilities?
choices: He has great aspirations and confidence in them.
He wants them to start companies.
quiz.explain: He says they have great aspirations and confidence in what their kids can do.

quiz.q: Why does he put constraints in place for his kids?
choices: Because kids can't just do whatever they want
Because the school asked him to
quiz.explain: He says, "You can't just run around the city doing whatever you want."

quiz.q: What do good founders constantly do, according to him?
choices: React to the market and new data
quiz.explain: He says good founders are constantly reacting to the market and to data coming in.

quiz.q: Why can he be flexible in the moment?
choices: He has values that act like guardrails.
He has a lot of free time.
quiz.explain: The values give him guardrails and a system, so he can be flexible.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: Act decisively, be willing to be wrong,
be willing to fail,
take chances, be generally optimistic, but also incredibly pragmatic.
One of the keys to my
success is I'm both like optimistic
and believe in all the things
I pitch and sell and whatever,
but also like know that you got
to be able to execute and deliver.
When we think about raising our kids,
we both have these like great aspirations
and confidence in what they can do,
but also are like,
"Okay, you can't just run around
the city doing whatever you want."
Like we have to put constraints in place.
I think good founders are constantly reacting to the market
and reacting to data that's coming in.
And so like don't be overly dogmatic.
So I think we're just very flexible.
And I think the values really help that, right?
Because you can say, well,
I can be flexible in the moment,
because I kind of have these guardrails
and this system in place.

lessons.speaker: Sam Yagan
lessons.title: Putting Family Values on the Wall and Into Practice
lessons.title_ja: 家族のバリューを掲げて実践する

vocab.ja: 認める・感謝を伝える

quiz.q: What is different about most families' values, according to the speaker?
choices: Their values are not written down on the wall.
Their values are the same as company values.
quiz.explain: He says most families have values, but they are not written on the wall.

quiz.q: What is the first thing his family does in the weekly family meeting?
quiz.explain: The first thing they do is what they call value shout-outs.

quiz.q: What do they ask instead of asking about grades?
choices: "Did you do your best in that class?"
quiz.explain: They don't talk about grades; they ask if the kids did their best.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an example of a "vanity metric" he mentions?
quiz.explain: He lists net worth, titles and GPAs as vanity metrics; doing your best is what really matters.

quiz.q: What does he say matters most about corporate values?
quiz.explain: He says the exact values are less important than really living them.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: Almost every company has values,
but I actually think most families have values,
but not written down on the wall.
They're integrated to their family lives.
And so, we have a weekly family meeting.
The first thing we do in family
meeting is what we call value shout-outs.
Everyone goes around and shouts out or acknowledges or recognizes
a time when if someone in the family did something
that lived by one of the family values.
We don't talk about what grades our kids get.
We talk about,
"Did you do your best in that class?"
We really try to focus on what's important
and not these sort of like vanity metrics,
like net worth or titles or even GPAs.
And I believe the same
thing about sort of corporate values.
It's not as important what they are, the exact values,
and more important that you really live them.
You need to have focus
so that you can actually make sure
that you're integrating them into your life.

lessons.speaker: Sam Yagan
lessons.title: The Power of Being Kid-Central
lessons.title_ja: 子どもが集まる家をつくる

vocab.ja: 冗談じゃなく・本当に

quiz.q: Why was the family moving to the south side of Chicago?
choices: To be near their kids' school
To be near the speaker's office
quiz.explain: They moved to be near their kids' school.

quiz.q: What kind of house did they first want to buy?
choices: The biggest house in the city
A house for a relatively small family
quiz.explain: They wanted a house appropriate for their relatively small family.

quiz.q: What advice did their friend give them?
choices: Live far from the school for some quiet.
Buy the biggest house close to the school and be the place kids hang out.
Buy a small house and save money.
quiz.explain: The friend said to buy the biggest house as close to the school as possible.

quiz.q: How many of their kids' friends are at the house on an average day?
quiz.explain: He says on an average day there's probably six or seven friends there.

quiz.q: What has been the result of this decision?
choices: They feel much closer to their kids and know their friends.
quiz.explain: He says they have become so much closer to their kids and really know their friends.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: We were moving from the north side
of Chicago to the south side of Chicago
to be near our kids' school.
We wanted to buy like a house
that was appropriate for our relatively small family.
And there was this one house
on the market that was huge.
We had dinner with two friends
whose kids went to the same school,
and he said, "Oh,
the best advice I can give you is
buy the biggest house as close
to the school as you can,
and just be the place all the kids hang out."
And so we bought the house.
I kid not, on an average day
there's probably six or seven friends here.
All the friends know the code to the gate.
We've now got a table
where we almost always cook for eight or nine people,
and just expect there's going
to be extra people at dinner,
and we have become just
so much closer to our kids,
and we really know their friends.
Like we have really worked hard
to make our house warm and welcoming,
where the kids and their friends could really hang out.

lessons.speaker: Jacob Bank
lessons.title: Why Startups Are Actually Better for Parents
lessons.title_ja: 会議ゼロの会社が親にやさしい理由

quiz.q: What does the speaker call the "night and day difference" at his company?
quiz.explain: He says the fact that they have no meetings is the night and day difference.

quiz.q: What happens when you have four, five or six meetings a day?
choices: You are out of control of your time.
quiz.explain: He says you are out of control of your time.

quiz.q: What kind of company can have no meetings?
choices: A company with a strict boss
A company that is small and high trust
A company that is losing money
quiz.explain: He says it works if the company is small enough and high trust enough.

quiz.q: Where does a fixed, guaranteed, high salary usually come from?
quiz.explain: He says that, in general, it is likely to come from a big company.

quiz.q: What does he say is the only thing that's really safe?
choices: Building a network and skills that keep you valuable
quiz.explain: He says no job is safe; only a network and a package of skills and experiences are.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: The fact that we have no meetings as a company,
that is the night and day difference.
Because in any company of any reasonable size,
as soon as you have four,
five, six meetings per day,
you are out of control of your time.
If you can get into a world
where it's small enough
and high trust enough that there's no meetings,
that's, I think,
probably the single biggest quality of life factor.
If you need a fixed, guaranteed, high salary,
in general, that's likely to come from a big company.
What is a safer company?
A 10-person, fast-growing, profitable startup with a super committed founder,
or a 200,000-person company
that has said they are at max employment?
We have this huge misconception
around what's safe and what's not.
No job is safe.
The only thing that's safe is
if you build up a network,
a package of skills and experiences
that make you always valuable
at a wide variety of companies.
That's the only thing that's safe.

lessons.speaker: Jacob Bank
lessons.title: The Double-Dipping Dad Philosophy
lessons.title_ja: マルチタスクより一石二鳥

vocab.ja: ほのめかす・意味する
一度で二つの得をとる（一石二鳥）
大切な人と過ごす充実した時間

quiz.q: What does multitasking mean to the speaker?
quiz.explain: He says multitasking implies you're doing everything poorly.

quiz.q: How does he define "double dipping"?
choices: Doing two jobs for two companies
Achieving two goals in a way that helps both
Doing tasks as quickly as possible
quiz.explain: Double dipping is achieving two goals in a mutually beneficial way.

quiz.q: How does he usually do home chores?
quiz.explain: He says he never does chores without a kid helping him.

quiz.q: How does his daughter react if he makes dinner without her?
choices: She asks why he did it without her.
quiz.explain: She says, "Why did you do it without me?" because she wanted to mix things.

quiz.q: What is the secondary benefit he looks for in a task?
choices: Spending quality time with his kids
quiz.explain: He looks for tasks that also let him spend quality time with one or more kids.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: Multitasking to me implies that you're doing everything poorly.
Double dipping is achieving two goals
in a way that's like mutually
beneficial to each of those goals.
So, for example, I do a lot of home chores.
I never do any of those
things without a kid helping me.
Now, my daughter is like,
if I make dinner without letting her
pull up her chair to the counter and help,
she's like, "Why did you do it without me?
Like, I wanted to mix this or mix that."
And so, not only am
I making dinner for the family,
but like I'm having this bonding experience with my daughter.
I'm teaching her how to cook.
So, it's not multitasking in the sense like
I'm not degrading the quality of each activity.
We have this fun experience where we're doing everything together.
We point stuff out.
And so, that for me
has been like the critical technique,
which is not like finding ways to not multitask,
like do tasks worse,
but finding ways to double dip
and find a task that can have a secondary benefit,
typically of like spending quality
time with one or multiple kids.

lessons.speaker: Jacob Bank
lessons.title: "Imagine If I Did That"
lessons.title_ja: 大人がやったらどうなる？

vocab.ja: 身近に感じられる・共感できる

quiz.q: In his example, why is the kid having a tantrum?
choices: She doesn't want to go to school.
She is late for a party.
quiz.explain: He gives the example of a kid having a tantrum because she can't get dessert.

quiz.q: What situation does he ask his daughter to imagine?
choices: Him crying on the floor at Trader Joe's because they were out of his cheese
Him being late for a meeting
quiz.explain: He asks what would happen if he fell down screaming because the store was out of his cheese.

quiz.q: What does he say would probably happen to him?
choices: People would give him free cheese.
He would be kicked out of the store.
quiz.explain: He says they would probably kick him out or forcibly remove him.

quiz.q: What is the main idea of his parenting style?
choices: Bridging the gap between him and his kids
quiz.explain: He says everything about his parenting style is trying to bridge the gap between them.

quiz.q: What does he do when his kids act like babies?
choices: He treats them more like adults and makes it relatable.
He sends them to their rooms.
quiz.explain: He treats them more like adults, brings them up to the level, and makes it relatable.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: If a kid, for example, is having a tantrum
that they can't get, you know, some dessert,
I'm just like, "What would happen
if I was at Trader Joe's
and they were out of the cheese I liked,
and I just fell down
on the floor screaming and crying?"
She's like, "Really? What would happen?"
She's like, "Huh? Well,
I've never seen any adult do that."
I'm like, "Yeah, I've never seen any adult do that.
But like, what would happen?"
She's like, "What would happen?"
And I was like,
"They would probably kick me out of the store.
They might have to forcibly remove me."
As adults, we don't get to have that behavior.
Like there's real consequences to that behavior.
Everything about my kind of parenting style
is like try to like bridge the gap between us.
We're not living in two different worlds.
Like for everything you're going through,
there's some analogy that I experience in my life.
I've always found, at least for me,
the more they're acting like a baby,
treat them more like an adult,
and just like bring them up to the level,
and then yet make it relatable.
Like, I experience things like this all the time too.
Like, sometimes I'm late for things also.
Do I have a screaming tantrum on the floor?
No.

lessons.speaker: David Reich
lessons.title: The Parenting Admin Problem That Inspired an AI Company
lessons.title_ja: 子育ての事務をAIに任せる

vocab.ja: 大切な人との充実した時間

quiz.q: What did the speaker imagine being a parent would be like?
choices: Reading, playing games and doing homework with his kids
Driving his kids to many activities
quiz.explain: He imagined sitting with his kids, reading a book, playing a board game and doing homework together.

quiz.q: What did he actually become?
quiz.explain: He says what it turned out to be was that he became an administrator.

quiz.q: How much time does he often spend reading emails, groups and apps?
quiz.explain: He says he spends an hour a day oftentimes reading through them.

quiz.q: What did he want to build with AI?
choices: A perfect chief of staff for every parent
quiz.explain: He wanted to build that perfect chief of staff for every parent.

quiz.q: What do parents get in the end?
choices: More quality time with their kids
quiz.explain: You get that time back to have more quality time with your kids.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: When I got into the parenting business,
I always imagined, you know,
you get home from a long day at work,
you get to sit with your kids, read a book,
play a board game, do some homework together.
What it actually turned out to be
was that I became an administrator.
I spend an hour a day oftentimes
reading through all these emails and WhatsApp groups and apps.
It's amazing everything's gone digital,
but it's become impossible to keep up with everything.
And so, I had the realization that I needed help.
Realized that AI could really jump in
and solve the problem.
And wanted to build
that perfect chief of staff for every parent
that you could really rely on,
so that it could take care of
the admin side of being a parent
so that you don't have to.
You get that time back
to really have more quality time with your kids.

lessons.speaker: David Reich
lessons.title: The Founder's Guide to Talking About Fatherhood
lessons.title_ja: 仕事は人生の一部にすぎない

quiz.q: What kind of team does the speaker talk about?
choices: A large team that works long hours
A solid team where people care about each other
A remote team that never meets
A new team with no rules
quiz.explain: He talks about a solid team with a close relationship where people care about each other.

quiz.q: What does he call one of the best things he has done in his career?
choices: Being happy for employees who told him they were having a baby
quiz.explain: He says being happy for his employees when they told him they were having a baby.

quiz.q: What does he NOT want to do as a leader?
choices: Make parents work too much at the wrong time
quiz.explain: He doesn't want to ruin kids' lives by making their parents work too much at the wrong time.

quiz.q: After having those conversations, what do you need to figure out?
quiz.explain: He says you have to figure out your system to make it all work.

quiz.q: How does he see the job or career?
choices: It is not important at all.
It is an important piece of life, but not the whole thing.
quiz.explain: He says the career is an important piece of that life, but it's not the whole thing.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: If you have a solid team
and you really have a close relationship
where you actually care about each other,
then these things happen.
And it's a two-way street, right?
Like, I think some of the
best things I've done in my career
have been just, like, being happy for my employees
when they told me that they're pregnant
and they're having a baby.
I want them to have that life
and I want them to have those experiences,
and I want them to be good at it.
I don't want to be on my deathbed feeling like
I ruined a bunch of kids' lives
because I made their parents work
too much at the wrong time.
So, like, that's not what I want to be for.
I think you just have those conversations,
and then you got to figure out your system, right?
To make it all work once you have those kids
and once they're growing up,
and especially when they're little babies.
I just think you just got
to do what's right for your life.
The job, the career is
an important piece of that life,
but it's not the whole thing.
And if you're looking at it that way,
you're going to miss out on what really matters.

lessons.speaker: David Reich
lessons.title: Don't Overthink Having Kids
lessons.title_ja: 人生を先に、仕事を合わせる

vocab.ja: 価値のある・欠かせない

quiz.q: What does the speaker believe you should put first?
quiz.explain: He is a big believer that you should put your life first in a lot of situations.

quiz.q: What did he and Sasha do when they were ready?
choices: They waited for a better job.
They moved to a new city.
They had kids and made the rest of their life work around that.
quiz.explain: They went and had kids and made the rest of their life work around that.

quiz.q: What is his advice to other aspiring parents?
quiz.explain: He says, "It's just, don't overthink it."

quiz.q: If you are a founder, who should you have a candid conversation with?
quiz.explain: It's about having that candid conversation with your team if you're a founder.

quiz.q: What should you be so that your company wants you anyway?
quiz.explain: He says to be valuable enough that they want you anyhow.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: I'm just a big believer
that you should put your life first
in a lot of situations.
Sasha and I knew since really
dating we wanted to have kids.
When we were ready as human beings to have kids,
we went and had kids.
We made the rest of our life work around that.
And I really think for other aspiring parents,
that's just kind of the right thing to do.
It's just, don't overthink it.
People have been having kids
since the dawn of time, right?
And they're dodging woolly mammoths and other things, right?
And they just make it work.
In our, like, cushy world here, you could do it.
And if you have a job,
even better, you could do it.
It's more about having that candid conversation
with your team if you're a founder,
or your managers and your coworkers and your company, right?
If you're working at a job, especially a 9-5 job,
and just explain this is your reality.
And be valuable enough that they want you anyhow.

lessons.speaker: Dan Beck
lessons.title: Adapting Expectations to Stage of Growth
lessons.title_ja: 成長段階に合わせて教える

quiz.q: What should you adapt the lesson to?
quiz.explain: He says you adapt whatever you teach to the person's stage of development.

quiz.q: How does he treat a senior leader?
choices: He lets them make any mistake
He holds them to the same accountability he has
He treats them like an intern
quiz.explain: He holds senior leaders to the same level of accountability that he is held to.

quiz.q: Why does he say it is easier to see as a parent?
choices: Parents remember a baby's early stages as cute
quiz.explain: Parents look back at a baby crawling and think it was cute, so they accept early stages.

quiz.q: How do we usually feel about an intern's big mistakes?
choices: We don't see them as cute or endearing
quiz.explain: We don't look back at an intern's massive mistakes and call them endearing.

quiz.q: What is his main message for the workplace?
choices: Treat newer people differently from experts with 20 years of experience
quiz.explain: New workers should be treated very differently from people with a lot of domain expertise.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: You adapt the lesson to be learned,
whatever it is you're trying to teach,
to their stage of development.
With a senior leader,
I hold them to the same level of accountability
as I'm being held to this entire organization.
You can't do
that with somebody that's just entering an organization.
I think it's easier to see as a parent.
You look back and, like, "Aw,
that was so cute when they were crawling."
But we don't necessarily look back at
that intern that was just barely hired
and the massive mistakes they made and go,
"Oh, that's so endearing and
so cute. Let's relive those moments."
I think it's harder in that work context
to kind of understand that same basic concept,
but it certainly applies.
We need to treat those
that are kind of newer to a job,
to a profession, to even just the working world,
very differently than somebody that's
been doing it for 20 years
and has a lot more domain expertise.

lessons.speaker: Dan Beck
lessons.title: Founder Mindset vs. Marriage Mindset
lessons.title_ja: 家族は直すものじゃない

quiz.q: What does 'to a hammer, everything's a nail' mean here?
choices: He used the same entrepreneur approach for everything
He liked building things at home
He fixed things in his house
quiz.explain: He approached everything, including family, with the same drive he used as an entrepreneur.

quiz.q: What trap does he warn about?
choices: Thinking you know all the answers after success
quiz.explain: Successful entrepreneurs can think 'I know all the answers', which he calls a dangerous trap.

quiz.q: What was he pushing onto his family?
choices: His own ideas of success and happiness
quiz.explain: He was heavily imposing his own ideas of what success and happiness look like.

quiz.q: What does he now tell himself?
choices: There's nothing to fix; smile, ask how they feel and what they need
quiz.explain: He steps back and reminds himself there's nothing to fix, just to ask and let it be.

quiz.q: Why is this hard for him?
choices: He is wired to fix things and push forward
quiz.explain: He says it is the hardest thing for someone wired the way he is.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: I'm sure you've heard the saying,
"To a hammer, everything's a nail."
I approached everything with the same drive
and determination as an entrepreneur.
At some point, kind of realized the impact
that it was having on my family.
As an entrepreneur, especially when you've had success,
it's easy to walk around and be like,
"I know all the answers.
If everybody did this, if everybody was more like me,
the world would be so much better."
That's a really dangerous trap.
It took me a while to realize the toll
and the impact that it was having on the family.
I was very heavily imposing my ideas
of what success and what happiness looks like for myself
and pushing that onto my family.
And so, it's taken me a while,
and I still have to step back and be like,
"There's nothing to fix here, Dan.
Like, just smile, ask them how they're feeling,
and ask them what they need, and let it be."
That is the hardest thing
for somebody who's wired the way
that I'm wired to do.

lessons.speaker: Dan Beck
lessons.title: Stop Trying to Fix Your Kid's Feelings
lessons.title_ja: 子どもの気持ちを直そうとしない

vocab.ja: それがどこから来ているか
その気持ちにすぐ手を出さず寄り添う

quiz.q: What does his son tell him about?
choices: Some really big, kind of scary feelings
quiz.explain: His 13-year-old son has some really big, kind of scary feelings, and he tells his dad about them.

quiz.q: What is his first reaction as a parent?
choices: He wants to fix the feeling
He asks a teacher for help
quiz.explain: He thinks, "I don't want you to feel that way. How do I fix this feeling?"

quiz.q: What happens if you jump to fixing something without understanding the feeling?
choices: Your son feels better right away
You don't really learn the lesson
quiz.explain: If you don't take time to understand the feeling and where it's coming from, you don't really learn the lesson.

quiz.q: Why is removing the feeling from his son a problem?
choices: It costs a lot of money
It robs his son of an opportunity for growth
quiz.explain: He realizes that removing the feeling is robbing his son of an opportunity and of growth.

quiz.q: What does he admit about "sitting in that feeling"?
choices: He doesn't know exactly what it means, and it is the hardest thing for him
It is very easy for him
He learned it from his son
He does it at work every day
quiz.explain: People tell him to sit in the feeling, but he doesn't know exactly what that means. It is the hardest thing for him to do.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: My middle son, he's 13
and just going through puberty and junior high,
and he has some really big, kind of scary feelings,
and he tells me about them.
And as a parent, I'm like, "Oh gosh,
I don't want you to feel that way.
How do I fix this feeling?"
But I think it's that relationship
that I kind of developed early on
where there's this association: bad feeling, have to fix it.
But if you don't take time
to at least understand the feeling
and know where it's coming from,
and you just jump to trying to fix something,
then you don't really learn the lesson.
When he's talking about some
of the ways that he's feeling,
or that he feels lonely, or something of that nature,
I try to remove that feeling from him.
I have to realize that's robbing him of an opportunity,
that's robbing him of growth.
And so instead,
just trying to sit in that feeling with him.
And I say that
because that's what people tell me to do,
but I don't know exactly what that means.
That is the hardest thing for me to do.

lessons.speaker: Jonathan Stull
lessons.title: Teaching Kids Agency in the AI Age
lessons.title_ja: AI時代に必要な主体性

vocab.ja: 言われたことだけこなす

quiz.q: What does he say is even more important today?
choices: Kids having agency, passion, and resilience
quiz.explain: He says kids with agency, passions, and resilience who push things forward matter even more today.

quiz.q: Why is 'tell me what's asked of me and I'll do it' not enough?
choices: It might not lead anywhere successful
quiz.explain: Just checking the boxes might not lead to anywhere successful.

quiz.q: What did he push his son to try?
quiz.explain: He told his son to play around with AI coding tools.

quiz.q: What does he say about using AI tools for coding?
choices: It is cheating and should be avoided
It replaces the need for fundamentals
It may feel like cheating, but there is a lot of opportunity, and you can still learn the fundamentals
quiz.explain: He admits it feels like cheating, but says it is where much opportunity is.

quiz.q: Why must people create their own opportunities?
choices: The world won't give you a playbook to follow
quiz.explain: There is no playbook, so you must adjust, be active, try things, and follow your passion.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: Having kids who have agency and have their passions
and are flexible and resilient and self-starters
and pushing things forward is even more important today.
The ability to be able to navigate
and find your own path
is going to be really important.
You can't just check the boxes and, you know,
"Tell me what's asked of me and I'll do it."
That might not lead to anywhere successful.
Even my son, who's, like,
learning to code, and he's still great,
I wanted him to do that.
I have been pushing him like,
"Hey, I think you should play around
with some of these AI coding tools."
Even though I know it feels like cheating,
it's actually where a lot of the opportunity is,
and doesn't mean you can't learn the fundamentals as well.
Being able to cultivate
or help your kids find something they're passionate about
and self-starters about, and have agency
and drive to do it,
I think has always been the role of great parenting.
All of us probably succeed
or fail in different aspects of it,
but I think it's ever more important.
It's just the world's not going
to give you a playbook to follow.
You have to adjust on information,
be active, try things out,
and then follow your passion
and create an opportunity for yourself.

lessons.speaker: Jonathan Stull
lessons.title: Walking Through Glass: Why Hard Things Are Worth Doing
lessons.title_ja: ガラスの上を歩く価値

quiz.q: Why do people keep 'walking through glass' in a startup?
choices: Because they feel it is meaningful and has impact
quiz.explain: He says you do it because you feel it's meaningful and has impact.

quiz.q: Why is growing revenue important to him?
choices: It creates the business around the mission
quiz.explain: Revenue is massively important because it creates the business around it.

quiz.q: What is the main reason he works at Handshake and startups?
choices: The mission and the impact of what they deliver
quiz.explain: He says the reason is the mission, the impact of what you're delivering.

quiz.q: What do you get from doing hard things?
choices: Joy and a deep sense of accomplishment
quiz.explain: Doing hard things gives a sense of joy and deep accomplishment, unlike doing something easy.

quiz.q: How does he compare startups to parenting?
choices: In both, the hard parts create a deeper joy than momentary happiness
Parents should not work at startups
quiz.explain: Navigating the hard parts of parenting creates accomplishment and joy, like in a startup.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: When you're building a startup,
there's moments you're, like, walking through glass.
You do it
because you feel it's meaningful and has impact.
At least for me, the business side of it
and growing revenue and all that
is massively important because it creates the business around it.
The reason I've been at Handshake,
why I've been working with startups before,
is the mission, the impact of what you're delivering.
So, it's worth walking through glass
because you're doing hard things.
And when you do those things,
you get a sense of joy
and of, like, deep accomplishment
versus doing something easy.
You can say the same thing about being a parent,
is like, there's lots of
elements of joy along the way
that truly are really just happy and fun,
and playing games, tickle fights,
and trips, and all sorts of things.
But, the hard parts, navigating that,
creates such a sense of accomplishment and joy
that's different than, you know, a momentary happiness.
I think it's hard until you've been
a parent to really get that dynamic.

lessons.speaker: Jonathan Stull
lessons.title: Four Concurrent Games: The Logistics of a Big Family
lessons.title_ja: 同時に4試合！大家族の段取り

vocab.ja: できるだけその場にいる

quiz.q: What happened for the first time last week?
choices: They had four games at the same time
quiz.explain: They had four concurrent games at the same time for the first time.

quiz.q: How long has the nanny been with the family?
quiz.explain: Their nanny has been with them for six years.

quiz.q: Why did his parents move to Walnut Creek?
choices: They moved out when the family had four kids
To be near their own friends
quiz.explain: They moved out when the family had four kids and have been really helpful.

quiz.q: How did they cover the four games?
choices: The nanny went to all of them
His parents, he, and his wife each watched one
quiz.explain: His parents watched one, he watched one, and his wife watched one.

quiz.q: What does he say parents are here for?
choices: To be there for their kids and support them
quiz.explain: Even with logistical challenges, he says the point is to be there and support the kids.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: We had our first day last week
where we had four concurrent games at the same time.
Even as they get older, as you know,
the carpool, the logistics, the dynamics,
and the parenting gets very different.
We're really blessed, we have a nanny
who's been with us now for six years,
who's incredible.
She also has a family, and married, and travels,
and so she's not living with us all the time,
but we structured really well.
My parents, you know, live in Walnut Creek now.
They moved out when we had four kids.
So they've been really helpful,
and also, you know,
that starts to have a different dynamic.
They watch one of the games.
I watch one of the games.
My wife watches one of the games.
I mean, really, I mean,
try to be as present as possible.
For Emily, that's definitely been a big focus of, like,
how do we make sure we're there for our kids.
You can't always do it,
and in particular with four you can't,
but make an effort to be there and support them.
So, I mean, there's all these things,
add up a lot of
logistical challenges on our side too,
balancing out work and the dynamics of it,
but it's important.
That's what you're here for,
is to be there for your kids, support them.

lessons.speaker: Ghazi Masood
lessons.title: Preparing Your Kid for Launch, Get the First Job, the Rest Is History
lessons.title_ja: 最初の仕事が、すべての始まり

vocab.ja: あとは自然に道が開ける

quiz.q: What advice does the speaker give his oldest child?
choices: Start a company right after school
Learn, graduate, and get your first job
Find the perfect job before graduating
quiz.explain: He says you want to learn, graduate, and get your first job. After that, the rest is history.

quiz.q: According to the speaker, what opens up future opportunities?
choices: How well you do in your first job
quiz.explain: He says how well you do in that first job opens up opportunities for the next step.

quiz.q: What does he tell his child not to do?
choices: Get too focused on what the first job will be
quiz.explain: He says, "Don't get fixated on what that first job is going to be."

quiz.q: What does "the rest is history" mean here?
choices: The past is more important than the future
After the first step, things will follow naturally
You should study history at school
Your first job will last forever
quiz.explain: It means that once you take the first step, the next steps will come.

quiz.q: What should his child use to get the first job?
quiz.explain: He tells his child to use creative skills to get that first job.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: The advice I give my kids,
and what I'm giving my oldest, is like,
Hey, ultimately you want to go learn,
you want to graduate,
and you want to get your first job.
And once you get your first job,
the rest is history.
Then it's like, how well you do in that job,
that's where it's going to open up opportunities
for the next iteration and iteration after that.
So I said, don't get fixated
on what that first job is going to go be,
but use your creative skills to go do that.

lessons.speaker: Ghazi Masood
lessons.title: Communication Skills Matter More Than Ever, Even in the AI Age
lessons.title_ja: AI時代こそ、伝える力

vocab.ja: 人前に出る・ふるまう
すぐに満たされたい気持ち
成長する・大人になる

quiz.q: According to the speaker, what decides whether you land your first job?
quiz.explain: He says how you show up is what will determine whether you land your first job.

quiz.q: What challenge does he see in kids today?
choices: They are too focused on digital things and quick rewards
quiz.explain: He says kids are fixated on digital and want immediate gratification from apps like TikTok.

quiz.q: Which is one way to become a better communicator that he mentions?
quiz.explain: He suggests doing things for the community and being more active and vocal at school.

quiz.q: What does he say about being a master AI user?
choices: It is not enough if you can't communicate well
It is more important than school
It is only useful for engineers
quiz.explain: Even if you build great AI apps, poor communication will not take you far.

quiz.q: When are communication skills important, according to him?
choices: As you grow and mature, even in tech
Only when you speak in public
quiz.explain: He calls communication a trait you need as you grow and mature, even in today's tech world.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: The importance of showing up
and how you show up is like extremely important,
because that's ultimately what's going to determine
whether you land your first job or not.
And I think that's a challenge today
with the world we live in with kids,
where they're so fixated on digital
and they have that immediate need for gratification
of like TikTok, Snapchat, things like that.
They forget how to communicate out there.
I think there's other ways you
can effectively be a better communicator, right?
That could be doing stuff for the community, right?
Doing something more in your school
and just being much more vocal,
and our communication skills is a trait
that you have to have
as you grow and mature,
even in the tech world we live in today.
You could be the master AI user of technology
and create your best AI apps and do that,
but if you can't communicate well
and you don't show up well,
that's not going to take you pretty far.

lessons.speaker: Ghazi Masood
lessons.title: Don't Push Your Teen to Work at McDonald's, Get Them Building
lessons.title_ja: 10代は「働く」より「作る」へ

quiz.q: Which job did the speaker NOT mention having as a kid?
quiz.explain: He worked in a restaurant, bagged groceries, and did car washes. He did not mention newspapers.

quiz.q: What does he think about service jobs?
choices: They are a waste of time
quiz.explain: He says those jobs teach different skill sets that are lifelong skills.

quiz.q: What was the main point of his post?
choices: Technology today lets teens use their time more productively
Teenagers should not work at all
Restaurants are bad places to work
quiz.explain: He says teens can now use technology to spend their time in more productive ways.

quiz.q: What does "that's not a knock to anyone" mean?
quiz.explain: A "knock" here means a criticism, so he is not saying anything bad about those jobs.

quiz.q: What does he suggest young people do with technology?
choices: Use it and experiment with it
quiz.explain: He says to utilize and experiment with the technology to see what you can do.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: I worked in a Mexican restaurant.
I bagged groceries, you know, I did car washes.
So I had all those jobs
as a kid growing up, right?
And that's not a knock to anyone.
I think those jobs teach you
different skill sets that are lifelong skills,
and those should definitely be there.
My point of the post was
there is technology available to you today
that if you're a young teenager,
you could be spending your time in different ways
and being much more productive than perhaps
you could have been in the past.
You utilize and experiment with that to see.

lessons.speaker: Amit Shah
lessons.title: The Move the Ball Forward Philosophy
lessons.title_ja: とにかく次の一手を進める

vocab.ja: とてもいい状況にある

quiz.q: What does "move the ball forward" mean in his family?
choices: Doing the next thing that needs to happen
Planning the whole week in advance
quiz.explain: He says you look at the next thing that needs to happen and just move it forward.

quiz.q: Who does the next task, according to the speaker?
choices: Whoever is in the best position
quiz.explain: He says whoever is in pole position tries to do the next thing.

quiz.q: What would happen if they didn't have this approach?
choices: A lot more things would get dropped
The kids would be late every day
They would argue more about money
quiz.explain: He says both of them are busy, and without it a lot more would get dropped.

quiz.q: What does he say about questioning the last step?
choices: They write it down every day
quiz.explain: If you get plugged in, you have enough context, so there is not much questioning of the last step.

quiz.q: Why don't they worry much if the kids wear the wrong thing to school?
choices: The kids pick their own clothes anyway
They buy new clothes every week
quiz.explain: The kids are young, and he adds that they let the kids pick their own clothes.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: Bijul and I both know what needs to get done.
Whoever's in pole position tries to do the next thing.
It's like, hey,
the next thing is Samir's got to brush her hair.
We got to keep moving.
And so that is the very physical
daily manifestation of move the ball forward.
What the next thing
that needs to happen is, just move it.
Move it forward.
Both of us are busy,
where if we didn't have that,
I feel like a lot more would get dropped.
I'm not saying things don't get dropped,
but there's a little bit of,
if you get plugged in,
you have enough context to do the next thing.
There's not that much questioning of the last step.
And we're in a very nice spot.
Our kids are four and two,
so it's like
if they're wearing the wrong thing to school,
Bijul's not like,
"I can't believe you put them in whatever."
Also, we let the kids pick their own clothes.

lessons.speaker: Amit Shah
lessons.title: Work on Yourself to Work on Your Kids
lessons.title_ja: 子どもは親の背中を見ている

vocab.ja: 自然に身につけている

quiz.q: What does the speaker ask his kids at the end of the day?
choices: An example of when they were kind
quiz.explain: He asks his kids for an example of when they were kind, and he shares one too.

quiz.q: How does he feel when he can't find examples of his own kindness?
quiz.explain: He says that when he doesn't have many examples, he is embarrassed.

quiz.q: What does he notice about himself as a dad?
choices: He wants the same things for his kids as for himself
He has no time for his kids
He is stricter than his own dad
What he wants for his kids is a little different from how he acts
quiz.explain: He says what he wants for his kids is slightly different from the way he shows up in the world.

quiz.q: What does he believe kids pick up from their parents?
choices: Both what parents do and what they say
Only what they see on TV
quiz.explain: He is confident the kids pick up what he does in equal parts with what he says.

quiz.q: Why does he want to improve himself?
choices: To show his kids curiosity and persistence
quiz.explain: If he is not curious and persistent about improving himself, he can't really show those qualities to his kids.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: I will tell you, at the end of the day,
when I ask my kids an
example of when they were kind,
it's very helpful for me to share
an example of when I was kind.
And when I reflect on the day
and I find that I don't have
that many examples, I'm embarrassed.
I have found that as a dad,
what I want for my kids
is slightly different than the way
I show up in the world.
And I think that a relatively
unhealthy thing for me to do
would be to ignore that.
I look back on my life,
turns out I did what my dad said.
If I reflect on the type of person I am,
I'm more similar to what he did.
I'm pretty confident the kids
are picking up what I do
in equal parts with what I say.
If I don't endeavor to be
better at the things I do,
how much curiosity and persistence is actually there
if I'm not curious
and persistent to improve myself, you know?

lessons.speaker: Amit Shah
lessons.title: The Week Bijul Became CEO (On Maternity Leave)
lessons.title_ja: 妻が育休中にCEOになった年

quiz.q: When did Bijul become the CEO?
choices: After they had their second child
When their first child started school
quiz.explain: He says Bijul became the CEO after they had their second child.

quiz.q: How does he describe the second half of that year?
quiz.explain: He says they really limped through the back half of that year.

quiz.q: Why didn't they plan carefully at first?
choices: They didn't think it was important
Their parents did everything for them
The company told them not to
quiz.explain: He says it was happening so fast that they just did it.

quiz.q: What did they decide toward the end of the year?
choices: To move to a new city
To rethink child care and how they use their time and resources
quiz.explain: They decided to invest and rethink child care and what they spend their time and resources on.

quiz.q: What does their support system start with?
choices: A nanny and a house manager
quiz.explain: He says their support system starts with a nanny and a house manager.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: Bijul became the CEO after we had our second child,
and it was a little bit of an urgent situation.
She was, by the way,
on maternity leave at the time,
and I had just gone
back to work from maternity leave,
and so we really limped through the
back half of that year a little bit.
We didn't take the time to figure
out what we needed to make that happen.
It was happening so fast, we just did it.
And towards the end of that year,
we made a pretty conscious decision
that we were like, "Hey,
we just need to invest in this,
to the conscious decision-making point of, like,
if we want all of this to be true,
we need to rethink how we think about child care
and what we're spending our time and resources on."
We have an incredible support system
that starts with a nanny, house manager.

lessons.speaker: Ankit Gupta
lessons.title: How Founders Should Actually Prepare for Kids
lessons.title_ja: 親になる創業者へ：時間の作り方

quiz.q: What should a founder who is about to become a parent think about?
choices: Where the time for parenting will come from
How to hire a new CEO
quiz.explain: He says you need to think about where the time for parenting is going to come from.

quiz.q: What does he say about decisions that are blocked on you?
choices: They should all go to your spouse
quiz.explain: He says the least amount of decisions that are blocked on you, the better.

quiz.q: What does "figurehead" mean here?
choices: A leader who is not involved in daily work
A person who works the longest hours
quiz.explain: A figurehead is the leader at the top who does not do the day-to-day work.

quiz.q: What can you do if you have excess time?
quiz.explain: He says if you have excess time, that's great, and you can fill it with stuff.

quiz.q: According to the speaker, what will most founders still be doing?
quiz.explain: He says you are most likely still going to be scrambling for time.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: If you are a founder about to become a parent,
you really need to think about where
that time is going to come from
for parenting.
There's probably things you do as
a founder you don't need to do.
Like, the least amount of decisions
that can be blocked on you,
or the least amount of, like,
actual day-to-day work you can do, the better.
Because that time will be needed for being a parent.
Try to take yourself out of
the job as much as you can,
and try to be as much
of a figurehead of a CEO
or a figurehead of an executive,
like, as much as you can,
in the most positive way possible.
And then if you have excess time, that's great.
You can fill it with stuff.
But most likely you're still
going to be scrambling for time.
But that time to parent and
that time to support your spouse
has to come from somewhere.

lessons.speaker: Ankit Gupta
lessons.title: Being a Founder Is the Most Family-Friendly Job
lessons.title_ja: 創業者こそ家族に向いた仕事

vocab.ja: 資金を燃やしている（赤字）
打てる手をすべて打つ

quiz.q: According to the speaker, what is the goal of a founder?
choices: To work longer than everyone else
To do as little as possible by building a team
To keep all decisions to himself
quiz.explain: He says the goal is to do as little as possible: hire the best people, set the plan, and let them execute.

quiz.q: What was happening to the company when his son was born?
choices: It was moving from losing money to making a profit
It was hiring hundreds of people
quiz.explain: He says Bicycle was going from cash burning to profitability.

quiz.q: Where did he join the last board meeting before his son was born?
choices: From the restroom of the labor room
quiz.explain: He says he did the board meeting from the restroom of the labor room.

quiz.q: What did he tell the board?
choices: That it was up to them to get the money while he was on leave
That he needed a new CEO
quiz.explain: He told the board it was up to them and explained how much money was needed.

quiz.q: What happened in the end?
quiz.explain: He says everything was fine and the company became profitable.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: The goal of a founder is to do as less as possible.
The whole job is to not have a job.
You hire the best people, you set up the strategy,
you set up the plan.
People are supposed to execute it.
When our son was born, bicycle was going
from sort of cash burning to profitability.
We had a great plan.
We were pulling all the levers, but at the same time,
we needed a little bit more money
to sort of bridge us to that gap.
The last board meeting before he was born,
I actually did the board meeting
from the restroom of the labor room.
I basically told the board, it's kind of up to you guys,
like, this is the amount of money we need
and either I come back from paternity leave
and we have that or not.
I had an executive team
and we had a great plan
for how to get the company to profitability
and you guys execute the plan,
but everything was fine.
The company was profitable
and you just can't do that in any other job.

lessons.speaker: Ankit Gupta
lessons.title: From CEO to Full-Time Dad
lessons.title_ja: CEOを退いて、専業パパになって

quiz.q: What did the speaker miss after he left his job?
choices: Problem-solving and a feeling of accomplishment
quiz.explain: He enjoyed time with his son but missed problem-solving, accomplishment, and gratitude.

quiz.q: Why did he become a full-time solo dad for a few weeks?
choices: His wife had to travel a lot
quiz.explain: He says his wife had to travel a lot, so he ended up as a solo dad.

quiz.q: How did he feel during those weeks?
choices: He questioned whether he made the right decision
quiz.explain: He calls them hard weeks and says he truly questioned his decision.

quiz.q: What did he miss the most?
quiz.explain: He says the thing he missed the most was some feeling of appreciation.

quiz.q: What happens at work that he enjoyed?
choices: People say thank you when you help them
quiz.explain: At work you help people with a task and they say thank you, which gives a feeling of accomplishment.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: I enjoyed spending time with my son,
but there was just none of that problem-solving brain usage,
accomplishment, gratitude.
We had all these plans to exercise, read, travel, whatever,
but now we were full-time parents.
So, it's really tough,
and my wife had to travel a lot.
I kind of ended up becoming a
full-time solo dad for a few weeks.
I think those were some hard weeks.
I truly questioned, did I make the right decision?
The thing that I missed the
most was some feeling of appreciation, basically.
You solve problems at work.
I love solving problems.
You're making progress, you're solving problems,
you're talking to someone, you're helping them overcome a task,
they actually say thank you, or whatever.
There's a lot of this
interpersonal kind of feeling of accomplishment.

quiz.q: According to the speaker, what is the hard part of training a model?

quiz.q: How many rounds do you need for decent training?
quiz.explain: He says you want to do thousands of rounds to get decent training.

quiz.q: Why does the cost pile up so fast?
choices: Real tasks are long and must be repeated many times
Dad jokes are hard to write
The CEO must approve each round
quiz.explain: A real task can take an hour, and you have to do it a thousand times.

quiz.q: What example of a long task does he give?
choices: Preparing a pitch, presenting it to the CEO, and getting finance on board
quiz.explain: He describes putting a pitch together, pitching it to the CEO, recalibrating, and getting finance on board.

quiz.q: What was the $200 for?
choices: A very light test to see some progress
quiz.explain: He says the $200 was for a very light test to see the needle move.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: It's not that hard to do the training cycle,
but to know what happened and
then be able to, like, question it
and figure out where the cracks are and,
like, go back and things like that.
I think the more you ask why
and the more you're playing in an arena you know,
the better off you'll be.
It's time consuming.
So, like, to get decent training,
you want to do, like, thousands of rounds.
And so those rounds, even if they're 30 seconds long,
for it to fully process and things like that.
But again, most training is
way longer than 30 seconds, right?
It's not one half-sentence dad joke.
It's usually like, "Put this pitch together,
pitch it to our CEO,
and then recalibrate it, and then get finance on board."
That might be like an hour-long task.
Now do that a thousand times.
That's where the cost, like,
piles up very, very fast, right?
And even in my writing, I want to actually spend
way more time with this model and do,
like, another hundred rounds of training.
$200 was for me to get a very light test
to actually see the needle move.

lessons.title_ja: オチを見つけたら、言い切る

quiz.q: What did the model get really good at?
quiz.explain: He says what it got really good at was getting to the point.

quiz.q: What happens when you ask most models to make up a new dad joke?
choices: They give you something like a paragraph
They give you a short, perfect joke
They ask you for a topic
quiz.explain: He says if you give a model a topic, it will give you something like a paragraph.

quiz.q: Why does he call it a "mom joke"?
choices: His mom told jokes in a long, rambling way
quiz.explain: His mom would ramble, explain the joke, and add an extra punch line.

quiz.q: What did he teach the model to do?
choices: Find a punch line and deliver it
quiz.explain: He taught it that once you find a punch line, just go with it and land it.

quiz.q: What was the result of the training?
quiz.explain: The jokes looked more like dad jokes and tended to be funnier when he judged them.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: What it got really good
at was getting to the point.
If you just go ask any model
out there to tell you a dad joke,
it'll do one of two things.
Most of the better ones
will tell you ones that exist.
If you ask it to make it up
or you give it a topic,
it's never thought about telling it.
Tell me a dad joke about the Startup Dad podcast.
It'll give you like a paragraph.
I describe it as like telling a
joke like my mom would tell it.
So, a mom joke.
My mom, like, was hilarious
because she wasn't naturally, organically funny.
She'd just, like,
ramble on to try to tell a joke.
She'd always explain the joke, why it exists.
She'd add some extra part,
like a third punch line that was never needed.
I think they're all kind of good at mom jokes.
What I taught it to do is,
once you find a punch line,
just go with it, deliver, land it.
And it got good at that.
So, like, the shape feels
and looks a lot more like a dad joke,
which means when I'm judging
it for funny or not funny,
it tends to actually be funnier.

lessons.title_ja: AIの学習から学んだ子育て

vocab.ja: よく理解する・ありがたく思う

quiz.q: What does the speaker say matters, in both humans and models?
quiz.explain: He says the whole suite of ingredients matters, not just one thing.

quiz.q: Besides the joke itself, what affects whether it is funny?
quiz.explain: He says who the joke was delivered to makes a big difference.

quiz.q: What does he believe about each angle of a joke?
choices: It can be trained in a model
quiz.explain: He believes each angle is a trainable element in a model.

quiz.q: What makes the best models great, according to him?
choices: They are getting better at using all the elements and adapting to the moment
quiz.explain: He says the best models know how to use the suite of elements and adapt to the moment.

quiz.q: How did his kids learn a good sense of humor?
choices: Over years of making jokes and seeing people react
quiz.explain: He says it is a collection of years of jokes, reactions, and explanations.

lessons.credit: Clip: Startup Dad podcast with Adam Fishman (youtube.com/@StartupDadPod) — used with permission

lines.en: I think it makes me appreciate,
both in humans and in models,
the suite of ingredients matter.
It's not just, is the word play good?
It's not just, did you keep it inoffensive?
But it's also, like, who was it delivered to
will make a big difference on
if it was funny or not.
The punchline will matter differently
based on who the person is.
I believe that each one of those
angles is a trainable element in a model.
There are still going to always be art,
and I think part of what makes
the best models in the world great
is they're getting better and better
at knowing how to use the suite of those things
and figure out the moment
and actually be able to kind of,
like, adapt around various pieces.
Teaching my kids how to
have a good sense of humor,
it's a collection of years and years
and years of me making a joke,
them seeing people react to it,
them telling a joke and other people reacting to it,
me explaining jokes.

Personalized AI-written review articles, like Wirecutter

choices: To show reviews hold hidden useful information, like long sleeves
To explain why he likes basketball
To say he cannot sit in small offices
quiz.explain: Reviews like "he's so tall, shirts never fit him, but this one happened to fit" hold information that is not written directly.

quiz.q: How did the first version of the side project perform?

quiz.q: What did Connor first think a salesperson's job was?

quiz.q: How does Connor now describe the job of sales?

quiz.explain: A great salesperson finds people in companies that have a problem the product uniquely solves; he reframes it as a search problem.

lessons.credit: Clip: Code Story podcast with Noah Labhart (codestory.co) — used with permission

lines.en: We started the company Jan 17, 2023, right post-Chat GPT,
but really we were thinking
about all of this stuff before it came out.
I was working back
before I started the company
on this side project.
Do you know the website Wirecutter?
Top 10 best non-stick pans, things like that.
My family loves these products, right?
My uncle will spend 20 hours reading reviews
to buy a $30 pan
just because it's like a hobby,
it's like a thing to do.
So I was working on a side project
back in 2022
of hyper-personalized AI-written Wirecutter articles
that would aggregate up
all of the reviews on the internet.
You can't tell on a podcast,
but I'm very tall, I'm six foot five.
It's hard to find sleeves that are long enough.
But that information is actually captured
in people who write reviews who say,
oh my god,
I bought this shirt for my husband,
he's so tall, shirts never fit him,
but this one happened to fit.
And that information is locked up semantically there,
even though it doesn't say
that the sleeves are especially long.
And so I had built this product, again,
as a side project,
really pre Chat GPT.
It's like GPT-3 Codex, an 8,000 token context window.
And it took 15 minutes to run
and create a thing.
It cost $50
to do one of these little listicles.
And honestly, it was really bad.
But there was a glimmer there
of just this amazing ability
to take huge amounts of unstructured
semantically rich data
and pull some sort of interesting insight
out of it.
And I just fell in love
with that problem space
that I was looking around,
wanted to start a company.
Got connected to my now co-founder Austin,
and he was working at Ramp, doing some growth automation stuff.
And I was chatting with him,
and a lot of the stuff
he was thinking about
was a B2B version
of what I was thinking about,
except instead of for buyers, it was for sellers.
And I paused and reflected.
I was a classic engineer.
I was like, yuck, sales.
Before I started the company,
before I had done a bunch of work in sales,
I thought the job to be done
on a salesperson was rhetoric.
I thought it was,
how do I convince you to buy my product?
And that's totally not the case at all.
Actually, what a great salesperson says is they say,
the job to be done in sales
is to find people in companies
that have a problem that my product uniquely solves.
And then it doesn't really matter
what you say to them.
Yes, you have to communicate credibly,
and communicate effectively, and be believable.
But at the end of the day,
in kind of a funny way,
the economy is just us solving
each other's problems for money.
And when you reframe it as a search problem,
just a bunch of really interesting stuff
falls out of it.
It's this search problem
that historically was run by people
in this sort of organization.
The system was a system of people.
But with LLMs, and AI,
and really high-scale data and software engineering,
you can make a much, much better system
that gives you repeatability,
observability, scalability.

quiz.explain: It is a joke on a famous line: they did it because they thought it would be easy — showing their naivete.

quiz.q: What happened to the first Postgres system over seven months?
choices: It got slower and the database CPU reached 90–100%
It became too expensive to run
quiz.explain: It got progressively slower until the database ran at 90-plus percent CPU, then pinned at 100%.

quiz.q: Looking at the graph, what does Connor admit?

quiz.explain: The line went steadily up and to the right for six months, so "we should have seen it coming."

quiz.q: What did Connor do while Sam built a new approach?
choices: He optimized the SQL queries to buy a few more days
He moved everything to a new cloud
quiz.explain: He spent six weeks optimizing queries; each day of work bought them a couple more days.

choices: The cluster could not keep up with the indexing load
Customers did not like the reports

lessons.credit: Clip: Code Story podcast with Noah Labhart (codestory.co) — used with permission

lines.en: Sam, one of our founding engineers,
got me this amazing mug,
which says on it,
we do these things not because they are easy,
but because we thought they would be easy.
That highlights our naivete in the early days,
thinking that this was a reasonable
set of constraints for us to have.
And so we built the first system in Postgres.
We were like, cool, we're geniuses, we're so smart.
Obviously, the thing to do,
you toss it all in Postgres,
it's normalized out,
you filter over JSONB columns on the CRM data,
and then you do a join
over this web scale data,
this event data, basically.
And that worked
for our first seven months of customers,
and it got progressively slower and slower.
And our database CPU utilization
got progressively higher and higher
until it got to a tipping point
where our database was just running
at 90 plus percent CPU utilization all the time.
Very scary place to be at.
Oh my God, this is crazy.
Who could have seen this coming?
And then you zoom the graph out
over the six months,
and it was a very steady line
up and to the right
until it hit 100%
and then pinned at 100%.
So the answer was
we could have seen it coming,
and we should have seen it coming.
I spent six weeks writing and rewriting our,
we had this kind of query building engine
that translated customer queries,
the UI, no SQL,
no code SQL builder
that they would have in the UI
into this very complex SQL query
that would run against Postgres in the back end.
I did a bunch of optimizations for it.
I was really deep in the query planner
and what's the optimization fences
and how to get
the table stats to be just right,
et cetera, et cetera.
And that kind of kept us alive
week by week.
One day of optimization,
two days of optimizations would buy us
a couple more days at a time
while Sam was really taking
a new approach at it,
which was, okay,
if we're gonna let you filter
on any field on any record,
why don't we use
a reverse index over this, right?
So what's like the great classic reverse index
is Elastic Search.
And so we took all of this data
and we dumped it on an Elastic Search
and we built a new query layer on top of it
to generate these elastic queries
and use that to build these very complex reports
that our customers needed.
That was really the core
and the heart of our product
to run the automations
that I described earlier.
And I'm cranking away, getting us Postgres level optimizations.
Sam gets this thing out and it works great.
It works beautifully.
We're like, we're geniuses.
We solved this.
Seven months later,
growing very quickly,
20% month over month,
things like that and more than that many months.
And our Elastic Search cluster
can't keep up with the indexing load
coming into the cluster.

lines.en: And the first thing my co-founder Aaron and I
realized was that there was just gonna be
a big gap in between
what people wanted to do with LLMs
and what they were gonna be capable of
from a regulatory compliance perspective.
So we wanted to solve for that gap.
And we wanted to truly enable any enterprise
that sits in a regulated or regulated adjacent space,
think banks, financial services, insurance,
life sciences, healthcare,
and government, and defense tech even,
to be able to leverage LLMs
without fear of data privacy,
giving them complete control
with governance and administration features,
and crucially also providing observability into interactions.
So we built an application security platform
and we were able to book
a few large enterprises,
but that actually ended up being
not our final destination.
It was another blip on the radar.
For this being my fifth startup,
I always like to say that I would think
at this juncture
I would have learned a thing or two.
It turns out I haven't.
And I think we've hit every startup trope branch
as we've fallen through that tree.
And oh, we overhired at one point.
We overspent here.
We didn't do this thing here.
We had to pivot our products.
All of those things
that you hear so many stories about,
I think we've hit literally everyone.
And so I'd say come '24, about December,
we had to sit down with our team
and we said, listen,
if we stick the application security route,
we're gonna fail.
This isn't the right spot for us to land.
We're just not able to successfully scale
our customer base.
And what we ended up doing is
we took our security platform
and we combined it with a multi-model offering
where end users could engage with a chat interface
like they do through these
single model provider tools, Claude or Chat GPT
or Perplexity, but combining that
with really deep security tooling.
So the ability to have complete and total observability,
control over how data is treated
in exchange with these models,
whether that's data you upload intentionally
or data you're just putting inside of a prompt
and securely be able to provide
these regulated companies with the means
to deploy any model that they possibly could
without fear, again, of data privacy
with giving them complete control
over governance and administration,
of course, giving them that observability.
But also doing that
with a really delightful end user experience
so that the end users
that are leveraging this tool
feel like they're leveraging
any one of the modern AI tools
that is out there,
only it's contained within the corporate environment
so that their data is secure
and the exchanges of these models are secure.

lessons.title: Don't Hire Until You're Breaking
lessons.title_ja: 限界まで待ってから採用する
lessons.episode: S13 E2: Securing Enterprise GenAI: Data Privacy & Security Guardrails with Steven Walchek, Founder & CEO of Liminal

たまっている仕事・案件

choices: Hire as soon as they raise money
Wait until people in that role are truly breaking
quiz.explain: They need to see each other breaking — nothing left to give and something valuable being missed — before they hire.

quiz.q: According to Steven, what does "breaking" NOT mean?
choices: Working and grinding 90 hours a week
quiz.explain: He says breaking doesn't mean working and grinding himself 90 hours a week.

quiz.q: What happened after they hired a VP of sales?
choices: Within a month, he said he was breaking and needed to hire
quiz.explain: Within a month he said, "I'm breaking. I need to hire," after 13 demos in two days.

quiz.q: Why does Steven take every hire so seriously?
choices: Hiring is very expensive in Denver
A hire changes a person's life, and you can't just undo it
quiz.explain: He says every person they bring on changes their lives irrevocably, and letting people go hurts morale and families.

They ship one update a month

lessons.credit: Clip: Code Story podcast with Noah Labhart (codestory.co) — used with permission

lines.en: We as a leadership team have really decided
that we want to,
we need to see each other breaking
before we decide to hire additional people.
And breaking doesn't mean like I'm, again,
working and grinding myself 90 hours a week.
It's that I am physically
leaving something on the table.
Not physically leaving something, whatever.
Spiritually, metaphysically leaving something on the table.
I have nothing left to give
and because I have nothing left to give,
there is something being missed
and that something being missed is of high value.
A good example of this is
we just hired a VP of sales.
And I would say prior to hiring him,
we'd parted ways with our last salesperson
and it was just Michelle,
our chief business officer,
and Maddie who runs channel for us
and then Julie
who heads customer success for us.
And the three of them
are servicing well over 40 customers
and also Michelle's turning on our channel.
They ended up lighting up our funnel.
We have this huge backlog of opportunities
and she's, I physically,
we're leaving money on the table.
We're losing money.
Like because we don't have enough of my time
during the day, of our time during the day,
to pitch and close.
So we hired a VP of sales
and within a month,
he said, I'm breaking.
I need to hire and he's right.
He's got just today and yesterday,
he had 13 demos between these two days.
Not to mention a whole host of companies
that are currently in proof of concept
and a host of customers that are currently expanding.
That's a lot for one person,
let alone a team of people.
Of course, all of us are supporting him,
but money's being left
on the table in that case.
When we're not serving our customers
to the best of our ability.
So at that juncture, that's the thing that,
I'd say that's the hardest part
is getting hiring right.
And for us, we've just made a rule
that we're not gonna hire
until we're truly well and broken in that role.
And once we find that we're breaking,
hopefully we've got a backlog of candidates
that we've either spoken to
or worked with prior to
that we wanna bring into the fold here.
And thankfully, it is certainly for this sales role
that we're about to open up here.
Brant, our VP of Sales, has a great network
and people that are ready to join.
So yeah, getting that right
is always a nightmare, Noah,
from a scaling perspective.
Every person we bring on here,
we're changing their lives irrevocably.
We can't just undo a hire.
And if you do,
you're firing that person or you're letting them go,
you're laying them off and that hurts morale,
it hurts that person's life, it hurts their family,
it hurts their ambitions.
That's something that we don't take lightly.
So every hire here is deliberate.
Everything is really well thought through and planned.
I'm saying that like it works cleanly every time,
it doesn't and I've got plenty of stories
where it didn't work out.
But in this case, that's something that we,
we as a leadership team
are really committed to is not overhiring.
Because we've done it already,
we missed the boat there
and we don't wanna do it again.
Yeah, I'd say that's been our biggest challenge.
The modern engineering tools
have allowed our engineering team to scale
so far beyond what we could have done
from a velocity perspective even three years ago.
Like it's crazy.
45 days, our team made 515 platform updates,
features, bug fixes, updates,
45 days, a team of six.
That's absurd, that kind of velocity is,
and it's increasing, it's not going down.
As people continue to get more and more comfortable
in learning how to use our coding agents
in the appropriate harness,
like it's next level, Noah.
It's genuinely next level,
like it's been so fun to watch.
Like what a time to be alive
and in technology.
