lines.en: Brief is basically your AI product brain,
so it's really an extension
of your product team's understanding
and capability, their knowledge,
as well as an operator
that helps you extend the capabilities of that team.
This is all based
in my own background, of course,
in product management.
What I found, especially in the past six years,
in between starting my own startups,
I was a fractional chief product officer
and always at any company,
the process of building software changes all the time.
It changes between projects,
it changes between teams, especially more so between companies.
But what I found was the why
of why you build products is actually extremely similar.
It's the same process at every company.
You start with where you see the company
going over the next three to six months,
then to the roadmap
of what helped you get there,
then down to the individual features and capabilities,
then down to the build,
and then each of these, of course,
are iterative back and forth
that you learn as you go along the way.
But that structure actually was repeatable,
and that's what my consultancy basically did.
I helped companies operationalize that process,
and in doing so,
basically found that we would more than double
their engineering velocity just through helping everybody through
that entire process understand everything
that comes into building software.
And that's basically the inspiration behind Brief.
That's what Brief does for companies.
It helps them operate
that why along with the how
of actually building software.
So tell me about the MVP for Brief,
the first version you built, you created.
How long did it take to build,
and what sort of tools
were you using to bring it to life?
So Brief, we started actually at a different company.
The company previously was called Moxie,
and it was around AI-powered sales demos.
And prior to starting Moxie,
I hadn't really coded
in anger in about 15 years,
where I had been managing engineering teams,
but not actually a coding engineer working on anything.
When I was working on Moxie,
I picked up Cursor for the first time.
And for the first time,
I was able to describe the software
that I wanted
and have it come out in a reasonable shape.
And when I went around
and showed a bunch of people
what I was working on,
they all basically said I was weird
the way my operating process was for using Cursor.
And it's because I was using
my product management tools.
I've been explaining to engineers
why we need to build stuff for 20 years.
And I was doing the same thing
at the coding agent.
I wasn't like, move this button, center that div.
I was like, here's the user.
Here's what the user wants.
Here's why we're doing this thing.
And so Brief kind of grew
out of that process that I had developed
through initially copying and pasting
prompts out of a document,
then into markdown documents,
then connecting a bunch of MCPs,
actually building kind of a second brain
that could actually coordinate
with the agent itself at that velocity.
And then just got smarter and smarter,
add more intelligence,
add more things to it
so they could make better decisions
and continue to extend my speed
and understanding to the coding agent.
And so funny enough, the MVP was very dumb.
We built it in about three days,
and it was a log of all the decisions
that we had made around the product,
who our users were,
what they were doing, et cetera.

lines.en: Okay, Drew, as you step out on the balcony
and you look across all
that you've built thus far at Brief,
what are you most proud of?
Every new feature has a moment
where we dark launch
it and we are the only users of it.
And like, it's funny building an agent
that gives advice
because how do you build evals against advice?
That's not, we're not scanning medical records.
There's no numerical correctness that we're working towards.
Was this good advice
or my bar for me is like,
does it sound like me?
Does it sound like a decision
I would have made in that moment?
Does it express that opinion
the way I would express that opinion?
And I think as each part of the product
hits that inflection point of,
hey, this is actually really good advice.
I'm like, actually,
this is something I wouldn't have even known
because I don't go scan all of our competitors'
websites every day the way Brief does.
That's the stuff I get really excited about.
So we send out a weekly email.
That's probably the crown jewel of the product
of here's what we learned last week
and based on what we learned last week,
here's what we think we should
be focused on next week.
And it's, at this point, it's really good.
It actually really sounds like me.
It sounds like good advice.
I learned stuff whenever that email comes out.
So those, the fact
that it took a lot of work,
it took all the underlying infrastructure,
all the agents, all the APIs and everything
to get to a point where it could have
that sort of 360 view of the organization.
But I'm really happy about how that came out.
Okay, Drew, let's flip the script a little bit.
Tell me about a mistake you made
and how you and your team responded to it.
The end of the day, Brief, of course,
was a pivot from a previous idea.
So I think understanding
the signals of what you're learning,
that the previous idea hit kind of a moment
where we were ready
to go asking people for money
and the money just wasn't there.
People were, come back next quarter.
It was basically the best response we got,
which for an early stage startup
means you don't have it.

lines.en: And so what we found was if you had
a good network connection for a little bit
and you caught some telemetry
and try to push it up
to a big database in the cloud, it worked.
But that really isn't the normal case.
A lot of time your network isn't good
or you walk from inside to outside
or into a tunnel
and then suddenly your network connection drops.
We were seeing
that the data was being dropped on the ground.
That still is the case.
We'll try it for a few times
and then drop it on the floor.
When you have those really frustrating experiences
where you don't have enough bars
and if you do have bars,
it's not working
and you can't get to your car
or couldn't see that it was there
or it wasn't updating,
that was when we lost the visibility.
And so when your customers
are having a bad experience,
they'll go to your big competitor
and maybe never come back.
So it's existential to us to have that visibility.
So the first version really was collecting all
that data onto the phone itself
and just making sure
that we could upload it later
when we did have a good network connection.
Sounds very simple.
It's actually really hard to do.
You don't want to blow
out the storage on the device
so you have to make sure
you're not collecting too much data.
You don't want to affect the user experience.
You have about 16 milliseconds before you start
to a human can notice a lag or freeze.
And so how do you do
and collect a lot of data
without affecting the rest
of your app's performance?
So a lot of the initial work
we did was around performance
and memory safety,
making sure that everything was asynchronous
and didn't affect the UX.
We had a lot of work on reliability,
detecting when it was working well or not.
So we ended up with a solution
that really wrapped a sort of native library.
We built it in Rust
and it still is to this day.
It gave us a lot of speed, performance,
and memory safety.
And so we wrapped that
in sort of native layers,
Swift and Kotlin.
So a lot of that work was done there.
And so that really was the use cases
that we were trying to do
were the Lyft consumer cases.
In fact, we actually were at the time exploring
writing our own native networking stack based on Envoy.
One of my co-founders had done
the server version of that Envoy proxy,
Matt Klein did that.
And we were looking at Envoy Mobile.
And so debugging a networking stack
and all of the varied conditions
that the network sees out in the wild,
that was the initial use case
that we started this on
and expanded it since then.
The other part that we faced
is where the Lyft
was still scaling quite a lot.
And so we had tens of millions of clients
on a daily basis,
like connecting and uploading data.
And so at that scale,
most of their solutions are too expensive
or they couldn't scale to that level.
I know we took down a couple of providers
when we tried to turn them on
past five or six percent.
So I think the other thing,
and they handled it by sampling.
And so the other thing
that we really wanted to solve
was being able to deal
with the mobile scale,
which is millions and millions of devices.

lines.en: I think early on we were our own customer
and so we had a lot of pain points.
I think the next thing we did
was we realized that we now had
reliable upload of a lot of telemetry
that you can collect.
A lot of that data
was never being looked at, right?
That's actually true of most observability systems,
like 90% of the data is never looked at.
It's only the bad conditions.
And so why were we wasting all this bandwidth
and storage and ingest
for data we weren't looking at?
And so the next thing we did
was add a little bit
of processing at the edge.
So instead of saying,
hey, I'm going to upload all these logs,
maybe I just summarize
or metricize them at the edge.
And so instead of megabytes of logs,
I could send very small counters.
Saved a huge amount of bandwidth
and really allowed us
to create metrics on the fly
based on what was happening on the device.
And so that was
a really powerful feature we added.
And then the next thing we did
was making this all runtime configurable.
Now, most observability systems make decisions at compile time.
You add a logline, you add a metric,
and that is done
when you compile and then you release.
You're doing 500 or 600 releases a day
on the server side,
which is what we were.
That's not a problem.
That's like a few minutes or 10 minutes,
like 20 minutes of delay.
On mobile, an average release cycle
was anywhere between 10 and 15 days.
You have your weekly trains,
you have your alphas and betas the next week.
Then you have to go to the App Store,
you have to get it approved,
and then it has to propagate
to everyone's customer devices.
So by the time
you hear about a customer problem
and add a logline,
all of a sudden
you had a really long delay.
And God forbid you didn't get it right,
you'd have to do that again.
And then after all that,
you'd have to turn it off at the end
because it was so expensive.
So the other thing we did,
and this is I think
one of the really things
that unlocked a lot of the rest
of what we do with Bitdrift,
is now we at runtime can say,
do I want this log or not?
For these conditions, for these set of people,
I can at runtime
choose what I want to do.
And so observability has now become runtime for mobile,
which makes it really nice.
You can say, I heard this problem,
get more information,
I don't need any more, turn it off.
And that's something
that used to take you weeks or months,
and now you can do it
in a few minutes.
So you combined like the local storage,
the ability to edge process,
and the ability to just be able
to turn it on
and control it from runtime.
We built that last part.
That really is the core of the platform.
And we've layered all the sort of
traditional observability use cases on top.

lines.en: So I know with Tribe.ai, you've been there
for a few months,
but I'm still curious of your time there
as you step out on the balcony,
look across what you've built this far.
What are you most proud of?
I never stand on the balcony,
who's got the time anymore,
but if you're going to make me do it,
I think about the pattern across my entire career.
I'm proudest of the systems
that are still running after I left.
DocuSign, I joined at 80 people,
rebuilt the platform through the IPO.
Our competition back then was paper.
That system today now still carries
the largest share of the world agreements.
At Stitch Fix, everyone talked about the algorithm.
I focused on digitizing the supply chain underneath it,
so the algorithm was picking
real inventory instead of guesswork.
Buyers stopped doing business over email and phone calls,
really major changes that impacted how people work.
So when I look at Tribe,
I know what it takes
for something to survive inside a company,
and I've seen it work across finance, retail, education,
supply chain, multiple industries.
That's the bar I want to hold
for every product we ship.
That's the way I think about the impact
that I'd want to create at Tribe.
We want to outlive the engagements
through the amazing products
that we're building for our customers,
so they continue to get more value from it.
That's the way I think about
when I do actually get time
to stand on a balcony.
Let's flip the script a little bit.
Tell me about a mistake you made
and how you and your team responded to it.
It's really easy to walk in and assume
that you are aided with the right tools,
you know the right technology stack,
you know all the development that has happened
that is going to change how you work.
At DocuSign, frankly,
I was hired to replace the platform
and I walked in thinking I really had it.
I had a new team, new city,
new technology stack at that time.
What I missed was really understanding
how people had worked with the old systems
and what are the norms and processes
that they'd established around that.
So when even the new system came along,
it was almost like organ rejection.
It was so much better than the last one
but I couldn't figure out
why customers weren't using it.
And what I realized was
I hadn't made the effort
of actually bringing them along.
Doesn't matter how good your system is,
doesn't matter how amazing your technology stack is,
doesn't matter how fast you got to production.
Ultimately, you have to bring people along
to change even if it is so much better.
And it's not just your customers,
it's your team, it's your people you work with.
To me, that's the biggest learning
is we as leaders are going to be
a part of transformations our entire lives.
Those transformations can be technology,
how you work, how you think.
Those things will always keep happening
but how you bring people along that ride
is going to matter the most.
And just knowing that,
just being able to call it
and being able to invest time
and bringing people along
is really going to help you
drive the outcomes that you're looking for.

lines.en: Okay, Pooja, let's switch to you.
Who influences the way that you work?
Name a person or many persons
or something you look up to and why.
Two people that come to mind.
First is, and I hope everybody knows about
Brewster Kahle. Brewster Kahle, founder of Internet Archive,
a legend in itself.
My first job out of USF
was at Internet Archive.
Most days it was early in its beginning
we just started this ambitious mission
to archive knowledge.
And it was just me and Brewster
sitting in a studio hanging out, scanning books,
and essentially taking on this job
of taking everything that was captured
in books, transcripts, old transcripts,
and then actually digitizing it.
I traveled the world with him,
scanning books in temples in South India
that nobody actually could even reach.
But the really cool part of it was,
despite them being digitized,
we actually built a mobile,
we used to call it, well, it was bookmobile,
where we built a van that could print
and bind them anywhere in the world.
The lesson I really learned there
was that digitizing knowledge was easy,
but getting it into people's hands is the product.
That's the value that we were creating.
So I think that was my biggest learning
as I think about my journeys, my professional journey.
The other person that I think of
is Tom Gonser, who's the founder of DocuSign.
And to me, the lesson I learned there
was that he started with the smallest possible problem,
people faxing signatures back and forth.
So much friction would just think, take paper,
sign it, fax it back, do the same.
My first project was literally
integrating with a fax machine.
To me, the big learning there was
that when you solve that one problem
and really create that sticky moment,
you get the license to rinse and repeat
that over and over again.
Your customer's going to trust you,
you can take bigger leaps,
and what is that real one small problem
that you can solve
that then gives you the right
to solve bigger problems?
To me, those are the two people
who really impacted my career.
I'm excited to be working with Jackie and Noah
now that are founders of Tribe.
They have the same thesis,
the same way to think about
how do you create value
with one use case at a time
and how do you create repeatability in your systems?
And I now get to be the person
who scales it out.

lines.en: The origin story is I had bought my first
single family rental back in like 2020, 2021.
And basically when I did it,
it was the worst process
I've ever been a part of.
And by that,
I mean I had tried
to do it as thoughtful as possible.
I got my realtor's license in Texas,
which for those who, it's 180 hours
of course work across nine full exams.
It's a pretty ridiculous thing to do.
And I was juggling that
in addition to investment banking hours
of 100 hours plus in a week.
So pretty terrible.
And then not to mention too,
I knew I wanted to buy a single family rental
because I knew that's the way to generate
the largest amount of wealth
in the most consistent manner.
And so the way that I looked at it was
let me buy this property
and I'm going to just house hack
and I'm going to move out to Dallas
for my job and the real estate group.
And I'm going to move from house to house
and rent out all the properties.
And eventually my net worth would hopefully grow
so much with the real estate
that I wouldn't need a full time job.
Now, that's the way it started.
But when I went through that first process,
there were 10, 12 different people
and sticking out their hand
and scraping fees from me
for seemingly holding my money overnight.
And I just thought this is absolutely ridiculous.
The amount of time it took me
to buy the property
and not to mention the fees
that I incurred along the way.
I thought there's got to be
a better way than this.
And actually had a month off
in what's known as garden leave
between investment banking to private equity.
And during that month,
there's a structural reason behind it.
But a lot of times people use it
as a way to rest, relax,
recuperate from a few years of investment banking.
I actually did none of that
and actually wandered the streets of New York
with a little black notebook,
writing down this thesis I had
about how you can leverage fractional investing
as a means to scale a massive platform
and ultimately become the residential platform of choice
where you're deploying products up
and down the supply chain of real estate.
So our goal is one day to become
that $100 billion plus company,
trillion dollar plus market cap one day.
But really at the end of that time
of the month off of jotting this down,
I thought, great,
I got that out of my system.
But it just kind of was eating away at me
when I moved out to Dallas.
And when I met my co-founder out there,
I was blown away by his background.
I had said, point me in the direction
of whoever is the single family rental master
around here, so to speak.
And I'd love to work with them.
They couldn't pronounce his name,
so they forwarded me his email and they said,
go meet Joey Guma.
I can't spell it.
Here's the email.
Ultimately, we started bonding.
He had grown Goldman's single family rental platform
from zero to a billion
in under 12 months with three to four individuals.
And when we were bonding about it,
thank God, he didn't call me crazy
when I called him to meet me in a diner,
pitched him on the idea.
And here we are today.

lines.en: That was a massive learning curve.
We made some pretty big mistakes early on
and so by that I mean
when we first got some funding,
when we first raised our seed round,
we decided we have to bring the technology in-house, right?
And we needed to hire someone that was technical
to actually start to progress this platform forward
because what we had candidly
was falling apart at the seams.
I wanted to move quicker after reading
all these books of how we move quicker
and so ultimately we decided that the first hire
that we needed was someone technical.
Now we went and we found someone
with an incredible background.
They had been high up
at a very reputable tech firm,
like one of the top tech firms out there
and we were like this is perfect.
This person can build out the platform.
We tested them through the interview process
and as a result of it we hired them
and they came in.
Now what we realized was
we were hiring based on the prestige
rather than what we needed in that moment
and what ended up happening was
we received someone that was very senior
at another tech firm
that hadn't really touched code as much
and as a result of which
we realized quickly that they weren't the person
that we were going to throw out the platform with
and it actually came all to a screeching halt
at our launch party
which was the funeral for the Monopoly.
And basically I can go into that story.
That was quite a harrowing turn of events
around there
but then we also hired out on the marketing side.
We knew we needed someone
to get the word out.
I didn't really have a marketing background.
Ultimately it came down to just who could you trust?
Who could you grow this platform with
and we realized
we made some mistakes in the early hires.
So unfortunately we had to part ways
and the person that we brought in
to lead our technology efforts
was probably the best hire we made.
Right out the gate, right?
And I had actually looked at LinkedIn
and went through every single engineer
in the DC like DMV area
and basically said who has a top background,
who has exactly what we're looking for
and actually cold LinkedIn DM
who would ultimately become our CTO.
When he joined, Claude code wasn't a thing.
Vibe coding was not a thing.
Cursor and none of that.
And he told us that this platform
that we had struggled to build for two years,
he could rebuild the entire thing
to the Figma designs that I had created
in a matter of a month.
And I told him that's absolutely no way that happened.
But go for it.
Sure enough month goes by.
He builds it.
It moves seamlessly.
And this thing looks beautiful.
We start launching platform assets
and all of a sudden I'm asking him things
and start to realize oh
you can iterate pretty quickly within tech.
You can do a quick AB test.
You can change this that or the other one.
Previously we would have to go to the firm
that was outsourced
and ask him like hey could you do this?
Can you do that?
And you'd wait a week
and they'd go through a whole process
whereby now we were moving
at the speed of light
shipping product feature updates
pretty much daily at that early stage.
And that's what really really conceptualized in us
the fact that A we need to move
as fast as humanly possible
and we need to leverage data wherever possible
to prove out this thesis that we had.
And there are ways to do it quickly.
There's ways to do it
in the longer term periods.
And so that first time
that I would say third hire
but real first true hire
that is now with us today
and actually became our CTO
was such an eye-opening revelation for us
that we need to hire people
for the seat rather than caring
about any sort of prestige.
You can use prestige maybe as an indicator.
You can use it as a way
to quickly sift through candidates
that at one point or another
they were at a prestigious X, Y, or Z
or they have experience building X, Y, or Z.
But we realized quickly
that you have to hire for the skill set
and what you actually deem necessary
and everything else is just kind of noise, right?

lines.en: With the MVP specifically,
Christian built it directing the AI agents.
And that's what we just divulged,
but I can't read the code, right?
So that whole emphasis of me
with the crayon drawing,
I don't know SQLite. I don't know Python,
like it's very crude understanding from my end.
So I wasn't even going to enter that realm.
And that's when Christian stepped in
and he thought of this genius process,
which I can share.
And it's pretty simple.
It's just a system of checks and balances.
And the reason
that we had to get into that
was because the AI will lie to you.
And we had oftentimes where we're like,
oh my gosh, we're done.
And it lied.
And for the first month
of us creating that MVP,
we kept getting so excited, so hopeful.
And then my brother would look back
and he'd be like,
no, there's so much more work to be done.
It's like a kid sitting
in the back of the car,
like, are we there yet?
Are we there yet?
Eventually, we got fed up,
as any young creator does.
And we go, no, we're building a system
where this just will not happen.
It's not a possibility.
So through all of those checks and balances,
and man, I got to say,
there's probably 20 of them by now.
They've been stacking up to the roof,
but thank God they have because without them,
we wouldn't be able to push a product
that we could verify, right?
We wouldn't be able to bring
anything to market with confidence.
So through that system
and that series of checks and balances,
and through learning and a lot of mistakes,
and especially, man, like you asked a story.
My buddy, he looked at my original MVP
and he can't even use Google.
I made it to look like a trading terminal,
a deal desk almost.
It was like he was looking at hieroglyphs.
It's like me trying to read code.
And he was looking at me
and he was like, dude,
I understand that this is the tool
that's going to help us make money,
but if I can't even look at the thing,
like you got to help me out.
He was basically asking for a lifeline.
And that was another huge cornerstone
of our design point,
especially where we're coming at,
because a lot of competitors,
we started to notice
that you just can't sift through anything.
It's a headache.
I need a Tylenol
after using some of their platforms.
And unfortunately, I have had to use
some of their platforms in the past selling.
So that was a huge turning point
for the MVP.
Checks and balances were a huge turning point
for the MVP.
And honestly, the constraints is the reason
the company even is able to work.
So funny enough with that,
again, it was just Christian directing his AI agents
and a lot of trial and error
to build the proper checks and balances.

lines.en: Okay, you mentioned being proud
of what you're able to accomplish with your buddy.
I'm going to give space
for a full answer there.
What are you most proud of with Stalex? Again,
I'm so proud that we thought
of not the lowest rank, not the weakest link,
but the guy who's
just now getting into the game.
The guy who he has no time
to learn a brand new system.
He has no time
to learn a brand new syntax.
Looking at a terminal all day
would drive him mad, right?
We built it for ourselves
because that's exactly who we are.
We couldn't sit there and just,
oh man, here's a blank slate of data.
Here you go.
Go get them, champ.
Or the worst part
is go find your own leads.
That's what my boss
was saying at that previous company.
He said, go find your own leads,
do your own enrichment.
And God bless, man,
my buddy was getting five leads
at a time using Chat GPT.
And then he would Google them
all one by one.
And I'm just, and we have
the connections to be doing this and more.
Why don't we use it?
So my proudest thing is,
yeah, man, we built it for the little guy.
We built it for the dude with no context
who has a great idea somewhere else
and needs to sell it to another business,
wants to sell it to another business.
Okay, David, let's flip the script a little bit.
Tell me about a mistake you made
and how you and your team responded to it.
A lot of them
and again pertaining to building those rules,
we had a review rule that caught a bug
and the fix for it broke something even worse.
And then it made the system print
the opposite of the truth to an operator
when we were doing a test run.
Huge fire just started from one branch going down.
And it only got caught
because of the rules that we learned previously
that a fix gets reviewed again from scratch
as if it were like brand new code.
So if we didn't have those things in place,
thank God, again, it would have been a mess
and potentially could have burned
the whole code base down
to where we would have
to do a full revert.
That would have been a full day's at least
if not weeks worth of work gone.
Big mistakes were learned along the way,
but they were always put out, man.
They were, it was always peaceable.
It wasn't nuclear in severity.
It was always like,
oh, the trash can's on fire.
Let's put that out.

〜を強く信じている、大切にしている
法律・規制で決められた条件
同じ所をぐるぐる回る（前に進まない）

quiz.q: According to John, what drives most of TrueDialog's feature set?
quiz.explain: He says that apart from compliance items, "it is 99.9% driven by our customer."

quiz.q: Why did TrueDialog decide to go narrow early on?
choices: Text has so many use cases that serving everyone means running in circles
They had no money for marketing
Their engineers only knew one market
quiz.explain: Text can be used for appointments, two-factor authentication, marketing and service, so trying to serve all customers means you "run around in circles."

quiz.q: What was their first vertical?
quiz.explain: He says "our first vertical that we were going to attack was education," starting with a for-profit university.

quiz.q: In the early days, how much of the roadmap came from that university partner?
quiz.explain: He says 90% of their features and roadmap came from the university they partnered with.

quiz.q: Which statement matches how John builds his team?
choices: He wants a small team of people who are all in, not passengers
He only hires people with perfect skills
quiz.explain: He prefers "a small team of people who are all in" and says skills can be taught but attitude can't; employees are also shareholders.

lessons.credit: Clip: Code Story podcast with Noah Labhart (codestory.co) — used with permission

lines.en: Our feature set and application set has matured significantly.
What we had today versus when we first launched,
it's almost unrecognizable.
On the roadmap, I'm a big believer in listening.
And we have very good collection tools.
And those tools are primarily geared around our services
and success teams and sales teams.
And listening to our customers
and our prospective new customers
with regards to what they're looking for.
And they'll tell you if you listen hard enough.
I think that our roadmap today,
we have some certain items
that come from a regulatory side
that the agencies require us to build in,
specifically around compliance.
That we have to make adjustments in our roadmap
and add to in order to fulfill regulatory requirements.
But from a feature set,
it is 99.9% driven by our customer.
And we got very narrow early on.
I think one of the phrases
that we use internally is that
when everything's important, nothing's important.
And that goes inside of sales.
I think one of the challenges
that I was faced early on as a CEO
was that the use cases of text
are so massive.
You can use it for appointment setting.
You can use it for two-factor authentication.
You can use it for marketing.
You can use it for customer service.
It just is so massive that
if you try to focus
and take care of all customers,
you just run around in circles.
So we got very narrow early on
and decided our first vertical
that we were going to attack was education.
And we got extremely fortunate
in that one of the customers
that we started working with
was a leading for-profit university.
And we sat down with them.
We listened to them.
And in the early days,
90% of our features and roadmap
was contributory by the university
that we had partnered with.
And they're still a client today
and still have an enormous impact
on what we deliver today.
When you say,
what does our roadmap look like today
and how do we build it?
It's 100% from listening to our clients,
where their problems are,
how the use of our application set
can be used to bridge the gap.
And if you listen hard enough
and ask the right questions,
they'll tell you exactly what's needed.
So I hear you saying we.
Tell me about how you built your team.
And what do you look for in those people
to indicate
that they are the winning horses to join you?
It's certainly been slow.
I think all things considered.
I think that what we found is that
we'd rather have a small team of people
who are all in
than a large number of passengers.
That's how we phrase it internally.
People that are just grabbing on
and trying to catch the ride.
What I really look for is work ethic,
intellectual honesty and integrity,
and someone who can handle ambiguity without falling apart.
Skills can be taught.
Attitude can't.
People who've lasted are people
who treat it like it's their own company.
And we take that position
and make our employees shareholders inside of our company.
And we want them having that owner mindset.

lines.en: But in my career, I've just been so fortunate.
I tell my wife constantly, I'm very lucky.
And I think that luck finds the prepared.
But early on,
when I was in college,
I worked at a restaurant.
And Chili's is still very popular today.
But I had a manager named Howard Kahn,
who was a general manager.
And we were the number two
or number three Chili's in all of North America.
And for a general manager
that rolled up his sleeves
and could do every position inside of that restaurant
and did every position,
he led by example.
And I think that in college,
I saw how he attacked things.
And he was a major influence
and mentor early on.
And then that led me
into my first job out of college.
And I got very lucky.
I had Axiom.
And I had one of the gentlemen
who was a head of one of the divisions,
a gentleman by the name of Steve Brighton.
And he was an early mentor of mine.
And I think that the things
that I learned from him with regards
to don't be afraid to take chances.
And it's his tenacity and effort and the culture.
He was a culture builder.
And I just really learned a lot
about how to build culture from him.
And today, I'd say
that my business partner is a successful investor.
People call their investors, my investor or my chairman.
I'm lucky in that I've got
a business partner who's also the chairman
and investor inside of our business.
And I think that learning from his experience
and his successes and the things
that he's taught me,
an enormous impact.
And it shows up
at every point along the way.
The integrity.
We had some challenges early on.
And finding a business partner
who shoots straight down the middle every time,
no questions asked.
There was a lot of litigation
in our industry early on.
And we got sued.
I think in the first six months,
one of our customers got sued.
And it was frivolous litigation
in the early days of texting.
There's the law that governs.
This is called the TCPA
or Telephone Consumer Privacy Act.
And there was a lot of gray area.
And it's since been cleaned up
through the Facebook Act of 2021.
And all of that's gone away.
But we got nailed.
It was quite expensive.
He looked at me, and I looked at him,
and do we pack up our bags
and call it quits?
Do we put our head down and march forward?
And he said, are we right?
And I said, yes.
And he goes, let's fight it.
And if you feed the pigeons,
they keep coming back.
And I got your back.
And he showed me
just what a true partner is.
And held his head high.
And doing the right thing, good things happen.

quiz.q: What question does every candidate at Harmony get asked?
choices: Where do you see yourself in five years?
quiz.explain: He says it is one of the vetting questions: every single person gets asked, "How are you a dog?"

quiz.q: What kind of place might a new hire be sent to?
choices: A big office in New York
A town of about 10,000 people near the border of Texas
A research lab in San Francisco
quiz.explain: They might be sent to the border of Texas, to a town of 10,000 people where half speak Spanish.

quiz.q: How did Brian reframe the challenge in his answer?
choices: He asked for a higher salary
He said these are important problems and US manufacturing needs to come back
He said he preferred to work from home
He said he wanted to be a manager
quiz.explain: He said these are important problems to solve, manufacturing in the US needs to come back, and this is the company to make it happen.

quiz.q: What does Brian say about judging if someone is a go-getter?
choices: There is a special test for it
There's no science to it; you need a sixth sense
You only look at their résumé
quiz.explain: He says "There's no science to it. You just got to have this sixth sense."

quiz.q: What is the difference between an engineer and a builder, in Brian's opinion?
choices: A builder only works on hardware
An engineer needs clear specs; a builder can work from loose constraints by asking users the right questions
An engineer talks to customers more
quiz.explain: An engineer can deliver on a ticket with defined specs; a builder takes loosely defined constraints and asks operators and users the right questions.

lessons.credit: Clip: Code Story podcast with Noah Labhart (codestory.co) — used with permission

lines.en: How do you go about building your team?
What do you look for in those people
to indicate that they are the winning horses
to join you?
So you got to be a dog,
and it's one of the vetting questions.
Every single person gets asked when joining this team,
how are you a dog?
And I'll tell you, when they asked me that,
I was a little taken aback a little bit
because it felt like a non-standard question
to be asked in an interview.
They were like, really, how are you a dog?
We're going to send you
to possibly the border of Texas,
where you're going to live in a town
that has 10,000 people,
half of them speak Spanish.
You're really going to be thrown
in the deep end of solving something.
How are you going to manage there?
And I said one word
or I gave them this answer.
I said, that sounds like some crazy dad lore,
and I am all for it.
And they got a laugh out of that.
And then I reframed it and said,
these are important problems to solve.
Manufacturing in the US needs to come back.
And this is the company
to help make it happen.
That's a part of our mission here.
We really are branded as the AI
operating system for American manufacturing.
It's not only a product
that we're trying to deliver,
but it's also an outcome
and a goal and a mission.
And circling back to
how that helps build a team,
you really just got to figure out if they're
that kind of go-getter. There's no science to it.
You just got to have this sixth sense
of who was selling you some BS
and who really cares about delivering on the product,
on the vision, and on the goal.
And then on the more technical side,
really have to distinguish
whether they are just an engineer
or whether they're truly a builder.
Because our employees have a lot of leash
and loosely defined constraints
on what they have to deliver.
The difference between an engineer and a builder
in my opinion is really
an engineer can take a ticket from Jira
or something with a whole set of defined specs,
and they can go ahead and deliver on it.
But a builder is someone
who can take a lot more loosely defined constraints
and deliver a solution by asking the people,
like the operators, the back office,
all the users the right questions
to really figure out what needs to be delivered.

lessons.speaker: Demetrie King
lessons.title: From a Vending Machine to Swipeable Surveys
lessons.title_ja: 自販機から生まれたアプリ
lessons.episode: S13 Bonus: Eliminating Friction in Digital Market Discovery & Deal Flow with Demetrie King, Founder & CEO of MarketMatch

vocab.ja: ゲームのように楽しくした
（意見を聞くための）消費者グループ
需要がある、求められている
名前やイメージを新しくする

quiz.q: What is Market Match, according to Demetrie?
choices: A marketing app that uses swipeable surveys for market research
A website that sells campus merchandise
quiz.explain: He says it "utilizes swipeable surveys to conduct market research in a gamified fashion."

quiz.q: What can students get for every 50 swipes?
choices: A chance to win a cash prize, school merchandise, or Celsius
quiz.explain: Every 50 swipes gives them an entry to win a cash prize, some school merchandise, or a case of Celsius.

quiz.q: What problem did Demetrie notice in his vending machine business?
choices: What he put in the machines was not what customers wanted
quiz.explain: He saw "a real disconnect" between what he was putting in the machine and what his customers wanted.

quiz.q: What happened when he put iced honey buns in the machine?
choices: They sold out the next day
quiz.explain: Ratings showed iced honey buns were the number one item, and they sold out the next day.

quiz.q: Why did he build Market Match as a web-based app instead of a downloadable app?
choices: Because web apps are cheaper to host
Because his customers said they would like it better if they didn't have to download it
Because the app stores rejected it
Because his investors told him to
quiz.explain: Customers kept telling him they would really like it if it wasn't a downloadable app.

lessons.credit: Clip: Code Story podcast with Noah Labhart (codestory.co) — used with permission

lines.en: So Market Match is a marketing app
that utilizes swipeable surveys to conduct
market research in a gamified fashion.
So instead of the usual Google Form
type of style survey,
we've created a fun tool
that gathers community feedback
in a fun way to help brands,
vendors before they launch,
place something in the marketplace
or spend money in the marketplace.
So right now, we're rolling this out
with a few different colleges here locally,
TCU, UTA, and UTD.
We are introduced a few different ways.
One of them is we actually come on campus
to showcase it to the students,
have them scan the QR code,
or the university will send a link out
for them to click on
for them to be able
to go through the survey.
For every 50 swipes that they do,
they get a chance to win some entry
to win a cash prize from Market Match,
or some merchandise from the school,
or even a chance
to win a case of Celsius.
We also partnered with Celsius
on campus at TCU and UTD as well too.
So it's a fun way
to get this feedback from the students
that really don't like the survey form type
that they feel like they're taking another test
while they're at school.
The main goal is to make this
like a very large virtual focus group.
So if anyone wanted to sign up,
they could go to a website, log in,
and then once we have a survey,
we can send them an email and say,
hey, there's a new market survey out
and we would love your feedback.
I started this because
I was an avid side hustler.
I still am,
but Market Match is my main focus now.
One of those side hustles that I had
was a vending machine business.
I saw that there was a real disconnect
in between what I was putting in the machine
compared to what my customers wanted in the machine.
Of course, as any business owner,
I'm not going to just buy something
in bulk because one person said
that they wanted it.
So I created my first company that started.
The name of that was actually
Vending MyChine, which I had people rate products
on a five-star scale to let me know
what was really in demand.
Got some great feedback from that.
Ended up seeing that the number one thing
that was in demand at the time
was iced honey buns.
So I just went
and bought a small pack of that,
put it in the machine,
and it sold out the next day.
And then I just started going down the line
of what else was really wanted, started selling.
Got some feedback from my customers saying,
hey, we wish there was like an easier way
to give our feedback instead of the rating.
So I went to swiping,
very similar to dating apps.
And then I had my light bulb, was like,
man, this could actually go much further.
So let me change the name
and rebrand it to Market Match
so I can use it for multiple industries,
not just for the vending industry.
Let's dive into the MVP of Market Match,
the first version of the product.
This would be post the original rating system, right,
where you started to move into building Market Match.
Tell me about that first product you built.
How long did it take to build?
And what sort of tools
were you using to bring it to life?
So it took me about six months
to build Market Match.
And I actually built that myself.
I don't have any technical background.
However, I am very ambitious.
And now with AI tools
that are out right now,
I was able to build
the version of Market Match
that I would like,
because one of the biggest things
that I was hearing from our customers
with my first venture was,
hey, we would really like this
if it wasn't a downloadable app,
if it was like a web based app.
So I ended up making this
using Claude and other AI tools,
saying, okay,
this is what my customer base is saying,
built, put it together.
And then we got it out
in front of the students.
And then ever since then,
it's just really been taken off.

lessons.speaker: Demetrie King
lessons.title: Ask the Customers Before You Launch
lessons.title_ja: 売る前にお客さんに聞く
lessons.episode: S13 Bonus: Eliminating Friction in Digital Market Discovery & Deal Flow with Demetrie King, Founder & CEO of MarketMatch

vocab.ja: 日用消費財のブランド（食品・飲料など）
メーカーが消費者に直接売ること
実際に見せる、披露する

quiz.q: What does Demetrie want companies to do before they launch or spend money in the marketplace?
choices: Come to Market Match first to survey consumers
quiz.explain: He says that if any company wants to launch or spend money in the marketplace, "they come to us first."

quiz.q: How do most brands usually test a product at Walmart, according to him?
choices: They put it in the store and see if it sells
quiz.explain: He says they "test out your product in the Walmart and see if it sells."

quiz.q: Why does he mention five Walmarts in a 10-mile radius?
choices: To show how big Walmart is
To show the value of telling a brand which store it should be in
To explain where his office is
quiz.explain: If he can tell a brand which Walmart it should be in before it gets there, that's a huge benefit.

quiz.q: What happened to the number one food truck at UTA?
choices: It got a permanent spot on campus Monday through Friday
quiz.explain: It was put on campus, got booked three times, and now has a permanent spot Monday through Friday.

quiz.q: Why does Demetrie think his surveys work well?
choices: Because they are very long and detailed
Because people can give their opinion without feeling like they're taking a test
Because they pay people a lot of money
Because only experts can answer them
quiz.explain: He says people voice their opinion "in a way that's not feeling like they're taking a test."

lessons.credit: Clip: Code Story podcast with Noah Labhart (codestory.co) — used with permission

lines.en: What we want to bring to the table
is if any company,
small, medium or large, wants to make it launch,
they want to place
or they want to spend money in the marketplace,
they come to us first.
So we can survey the consumer base
to let them know where they want to go.
A great example of that is,
say you're a CPG brand,
and you want to be in Walmart,
like with most companies, if you're a brand,
what they do is they test out your product
in the Walmart and see if it sells.
However, what we're trying to do is
let's not put it in Walmart
and see if it sells.
Let's ask the customers
that are coming to that Walmart,
is this something that they would like?
And it's not just about getting
the brand in the store.
It's also bringing more exposure to that brand.
So if the consumers on my application
want to go and buy for them directly,
that's also a great way
for them to get that exposure.
You could have five Walmarts
in a 10 mile radius.
And if I can tell a brand
which Walmart it should be in
before it gets there,
that's a huge benefit for that brand.
While I'm also showcasing their brand
to the consumers that are on my app,
creating a connection that they could either
follow them on social media,
they could become a customer
buying their product directly from being a D2C client.
Recently, we just showcase how this could really work
by putting some food trucks
on our app for UTA.
And we let the students
swipe to the food trucks.
The number one food truck
was then put on campus.
It got booked three times after that.
And now it has a permanent spot
on UTA campus Monday through Friday,
just from being on the application.
And that's another way of
if you give the consumer the ability
to voice their opinion in a way
that's not feeling like they're taking a test.
It showcases that we can put the right people
in the right places at the right time.

lessons.speaker: Marie-Pierre St-Onge
lessons.role: Associate Professor of Nutritional Medicine, Columbia University
lessons.title: Can Food Change Your Sleep?
lessons.title_ja: 食べた物で眠りは変わる？
lessons.episode: #552: Diet & Sleep Interactions – Marie-Pierre St. Onge, PhD

vocab.ja: 〜する知識・準備が十分にある
精製された炭水化物（白いパン・砂糖など）

quiz.q: Who asked her if diet could help sleep?
quiz.explain: The committee for the 2015 US Dietary Guidelines asked: "Can we make dietary recommendations to improve sleep?"

quiz.q: Why was she surprised by the question?
choices: She has a PhD in nutrition but never thought of the reverse question
She thought diet and sleep were not connected
She did not have any data
quiz.explain: "I have a PhD in nutrition, I hadn't even thought of addressing this question."

quiz.q: When people chose their own food, what did they eat?
choices: More fat, more sodium, less fiber and more calories
quiz.explain: Participants ate more fat, more saturated fat, less fiber, more sodium and more calories.

quiz.q: How was their sleep on the days they chose their own food?
choices: They took longer to fall asleep and had a little less deep sleep
quiz.explain: They took longer to fall asleep and spent a little less time in deep sleep.

quiz.q: Which was linked to more deep sleep?
quiz.explain: Participants who had more fiber had more deep sleep.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: But it was in 2014,
the Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee
for the 2015 Dietary Guidelines in the US
reached out to me
to talk about diet and sleep.
I was very well equipped
to talk to them about sleep,
how it influences your food choices.
You tend to increase your fat intake,
tend to have a higher intake
of refined carbohydrates, more snack foods.
And they said, yeah, OK,
we're making dietary recommendations.
Can we make dietary recommendations to improve sleep?
Huh, I hadn't even thought of that.
You're thinking one way,
but from population-based studies,
things could go either way.
And I thought this was very interesting.
And I couldn't believe,
I have a PhD in nutrition,
I hadn't even thought of addressing this question,
or at least looking into this reverse question
of can we, or can diet impact sleep?
So I decided to look
at some of the data
that we had from our sleep restriction study.
And it was an inpatient study,
where in one phase
participants spent four hours in bed,
in another phase
participants spent nine hours in bed.
So I was like, OK, well,
during the nine-hour in-bed period,
people have variable sleep from one another.
In the sleep restriction condition,
everybody slept very well.
They were very efficient with their sleep,
they spent most of the time in bed asleep,
but not when they spent nine hours in bed.
So in that study,
we had four days of a controlled diet.
So we gave our participants
all of the food that they needed,
as estimated by their energy requirements,
based on a healthy general diet.
And then that's when we measured
all of the metabolic outcomes
that we were interested in.
But then we wanted to know,
are they going to eat more or less
or differently
after a period of short sleep
versus adequate sleep in the lab?
And we measured their food intake that day.
So we took a very systematic approach
then to determine if there was
an impact of diet on sleep.
First, was there a difference in their food intake
when they self-selected their diet
compared to when we gave them their meals?
And yes, there were differences.
Participants ate more fat, more saturated fat,
less fiber, more sodium,
more calories in general,
when they self-selected their diet
compared to the diet that we had given them.
So I'm like, OK, well,
there's differences there.
Every night in the lab,
we measured their sleep using polysomnography,
so electrodes,
and we could assess sleep staging, all of that.
So OK, so their diets were different.
Was their sleep different?
Because if their sleep wasn't different,
then that ends the inquiry, right?
But their sleep was different.
They took longer to fall asleep
when they self-selected their diet.
They spent a little less time in deep sleep
when they self-selected their diet.
So I'm like, OK, well,
there's some differences in their sleep.
Maybe it has to do
with what they ate that day.
So then we only looked at the day
where they self-selected their diet,
because on the control diet,
everybody ate the same thing.
So there's no variability there.
And that's where we found
that participants who had more fiber
had more deep sleep,
the participants who had more saturated fat
in their diet that day
had less deep sleep.
And participants who had more refined carbohydrates
and more sugar during the day
had more arousal that night
and more light, disturbed sleep.

lessons.speaker: Marlou Lasschuijt
lessons.role: Assistant Professor, Sensory Science and Eating Behaviour, Wageningen University
lessons.title: Texture Beats Counting Chews
lessons.title_ja: かむ回数より、食べ物のかたさ
lessons.episode: #526: Eating Rate, Food Texture & Satiation – Marlou Lasschuijt, PhD

vocab.ja: 気持ち悪い、うんざりする
食感（かたさ・やわらかさ）
ぶるぶる震える、振動する

quiz.q: What did Fletcherism tell people to do?
choices: Chew a bite 10 or 20 times before swallowing
quiz.explain: It was a diet method where people chewed a bite 10 or 20 times before swallowing.

quiz.q: What is the problem with chewing one bite that many times?
quiz.explain: "If you chew one bite of food for that many times, it becomes quite disgusting."

quiz.q: What happens when the texture of food changes?
choices: People eat more slowly and eat less, without thinking about it
quiz.explain: People alter their way of eating naturally, without thinking about it, and eat less.

quiz.q: Which is an example of an external way to slow eating?
choices: A spoon that vibrates if you eat too fast
quiz.explain: A screen that shows when to take a bite, or spoons that vibrate if you eat too fast.

quiz.q: Why does she like changing the texture of food?
choices: It needs no instructions or special device
quiz.explain: "You don't have to give people instructions or a special device."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: I think this was in the 80s,
if I remember correctly.
You had Fletcherism,
which was a diet method
where people were instructed to chew a bite
10 or 20 times before swallowing.
And that worked,
but I don't know if you've ever tried,
but if you chew one bite of food
for that many times,
it becomes quite disgusting.
So I think it was also
largely driven by palatability.
And I think what's nice
about changing the texture of food
is that people will alter
their way of eating that food
naturally, without thinking about it,
and then naturally eat less of the food
compared to when they would eat it
with little chews and very fast.
Because there have been many efforts
trying to reduce people's eating rate
by more external factors.
So in a research setting,
we could have a screen
that indicated when to take a bite,
so there were longer breaks between bites.
There are spoons that start to vibrate
if you eat too fast.
There are all types of ways
that people try to reduce people's eating rate.
But I think the nice part
about altering the texture
is that it goes without thinking
in a natural way.
So you don't have to give people instructions
or a special device.

lessons.speaker: Danny Lennon
lessons.title: Your Second Coffee Adds Up
lessons.title_ja: 2杯目のコーヒーは上乗せされる
lessons.episode: Caffeine Metabolism and Individual Variability

vocab.ja: 覚えておく、心に留める
半減期（量が半分になるまでの時間）

quiz.q: Besides timing and the amount in one drink, what should we think about?
choices: The caffeine that builds up across the day
quiz.explain: Caffeine stays in circulation for hours, so we need to bear in mind the accumulative amount across the day.

quiz.q: What is the half-life of caffeine in most people, according to Danny?
quiz.explain: "Caffeine has a half-life of about 3 to 5 hours in most individuals."

quiz.q: What does "half-life" mean here?
choices: Half the caffeine is still in the bloodstream
quiz.explain: After that time, only half the ingested caffeine remains; half has been metabolized and cleared.

quiz.q: What happens when you drink a second cup of coffee hours later?
choices: It goes on top of the caffeine still in your system
quiz.explain: The second cup's caffeine "is going on top of whatever caffeine is still in your system."

quiz.q: Why can even moderate drinks cause problems?
choices: Having them many times a day adds up to a high level
quiz.explain: Having them multiple times across the day creates a cumulative impact that can get high enough to cause negative effects.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: However, it's not just the timing,
or it's not just the amount of caffeine
in a beverage at one time point.
Because caffeine stays in the circulation
for multiple hours across the day,
we need to bear in mind
that accumulative caffeine amount
that's in circulation across that day.
So, for example, if we consider
that caffeine has a half-life
of about 3 to 5 hours in most individuals,
it means that after that period of time,
only half the amount of that ingested caffeine
is going to remain in the bloodstream.
So half of it has been metabolized and cleared,
but the other half is still there.
And so multiple hours afterwards,
we still have that amount there.
So then if you go and have
another intake of caffeine
from another caffeine source,
there's going to have this additive value.
Not only is it the amount
in this second cup of coffee you're having,
the caffeine amount that you then have,
but that is going on top
of whatever caffeine is still in your system.
And multiple hours after your previous coffee,
you could still have half of that there.
And so it's this cumulative thing that not only,
even if you're consuming beverages
that contain, let's say,
a moderate amount of caffeine,
if you're having them multiple times across the day
and you have this cumulative impact,
At some point then you might reach this level
where the accumulative concentration in circulation
is high enough for you to experience
some of the negative impacts that you have.

lessons.speaker: Amy Bender
lessons.role: Sleep researcher, Centre for Sleep & Human Performance
lessons.title: Two Systems Run Your Sleep
lessons.title_ja: 眠りを動かす2つのしくみ
lessons.episode: SNR #209: Amy Bender, PhD - Sleep Better: Practical Evidence-Based Recommendations

vocab.ja: 睡眠圧（起きているほどたまる眠気）
概日リズム（約1日の体内時計）
上がったり下がったりの変化

quiz.q: What are the two main processes that regulate sleep?
choices: Sleep pressure and the circadian rhythm
quiz.explain: The homeostatic process (sleep pressure) and the circadian rhythm help regulate our sleep-wake cycles.

quiz.q: What does the homeostatic process mean?
choices: The longer you've been awake, the more you want to sleep
You always wake up at the same time
Your body needs food at night
quiz.explain: "The longer you've been awake, the more likelihood you will want to sleep."

quiz.q: How long are most people's circadian rhythms?
quiz.explain: "The majority of people have circadian rhythms longer than 24 hours."

quiz.q: How long did participants stay awake in her studies?
quiz.explain: Participants went without sleep for 62 hours, two full nights.

quiz.q: Why were people more alert at hour 60 than at hour 48?
choices: 8 p.m. is a time of high alertness in the circadian rhythm
quiz.explain: Part of it was excitement, but part was the circadian rhythm: 8 p.m. is a high level of alertness.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: So basically we have two main processes
that regulate our sleep-wake activity.
So we have the homeostatic process,
which basically means the longer you've been awake,
the more likelihood you will want to sleep.
So sleep pressure.
But then we also have the circadian rhythm,
which means about a day.
So our circadian rhythms typically are about 24 hours.
The majority of people have circadian rhythms
longer than 24 hours.
And so circadian rhythms,
they're independent of prior sleep-wake activity.
And so there's just fluctuations,
natural fluctuations in alertness and sleepiness
across the 24-hour day.
And so those two main processes
help regulate our sleep-wake cycles.
And just to kind of give you an example,
so in my graduate work,
I worked 62-hour sleep deprivation studies.
So we would have participants
go without sleep for 62 hours.
That's two full nights.
Yeah, two full nights without sleep.
And so what was interesting to me,
I mean, just getting started into the field,
I always thought about sleep pressure.
So the longer they've been awake,
the more likelihood they'll want to sleep.
But I didn't quite realize
the impact of the circadian rhythm.
And so it was interesting to me
that on, let's say, hour 60,
they're alert as they can be.
I mean, part of that is due
to the excitement
of being able to go to sleep.
But part of that is also due
to the circadian rhythm is just, you know,
8 p.m. is a high level of alertness.
And so when you compare that to,
let's say, you know, hour 48 or so,
they were more alert at that 60-hour mark,
compared to other times of day
when they aren't as sleep-deprived.

lessons.speaker: Amy Bender
lessons.role: Sleep researcher, Centre for Sleep & Human Performance
lessons.title: Do You Really Need Eight Hours?
lessons.title_ja: 本当に必要な睡眠は何時間？
lessons.episode: SNR #209: Amy Bender, PhD - Sleep Better: Practical Evidence-Based Recommendations

quiz.q: How much sleep is recommended for a normal healthy adult?
quiz.explain: "For a normal healthy adult, the recommendation is between seven and nine hours of sleep per night."

quiz.q: Why do athletes need more sleep?
choices: Their mental and physical loads need more recovery time
quiz.explain: The mental load and physical loads on an athlete's body require more recovery time.

quiz.q: How many people can really get by on six hours or less?
quiz.explain: "Less than 1% of the population can get by on six hours or less of sleep per night."

quiz.q: What happens to people who think six hours is enough?
choices: Their brain resets to a new set point, but they don't perform optimally
quiz.explain: Your brain resets itself to a new set point, but you're still not performing optimally.

quiz.q: Which is a good sign that you are getting enough sleep?
choices: Waking up without an alarm clock
quiz.explain: Good signs: waking up without an alarm clock, not needing copious caffeine, and being alert all day.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: So there's a lot of individual variability
in the amount of sleep that we need.
However, for a normal healthy adult,
the recommendation is between seven and nine hours
of sleep per night.
And for athletes, we think that they need more.
So we think we're shooting more
towards that eight-hour range
because of the mental and physical,
just the mental load and the physical loads
that are put on an athlete's body
just require more recovery time.
So we think athletes certainly need more sleep.
And there is a number,
less than 1% of the population
who can get by on six hours or less
of sleep per night.
So there are a number of people out there
who think, you know, I only need six hours,
I'm fine.
But in reality,
there is a very, very small percentage
that can actually get by on less sleep.
So your brain kind of, it resets itself
to this new set point.
But you're still not performing optimally
if you're not getting within that seven-to-nine-hour range.
And the range is quite, it's quite large.
So it's a bit difficult to figure out
within that range, you know,
what is optimal for me.
But I think some good signs
that you're getting enough sleep
would be waking up without an alarm clock,
not needing copious amounts of caffeine
throughout the day to try and keep you awake.
You know, you're alert throughout the day
is a good sign that you're getting that quantity.

lessons.speaker: Amy Bender
lessons.role: Sleep researcher, Centre for Sleep & Human Performance
lessons.title: The 20-Minute Nap
lessons.title_ja: 昼寝は20分、目覚ましは30分
lessons.episode: SNR #209: Amy Bender, PhD - Sleep Better: Practical Evidence-Based Recommendations

vocab.ja: 短い昼寝（パワーナップ）
仕事のはかどり、生産性

quiz.q: What can a 15 to 20-minute power nap do?
choices: Make you sleep less at night
quiz.explain: A power nap has been shown to increase levels of alertness and boost mood.

quiz.q: How long a nap does she recommend?
quiz.explain: "We recommend about a 20-minute nap."

quiz.q: What should you set your alarm for?
quiz.explain: "You would set your alarm for about 30 minutes."

quiz.q: When is a good time to nap?
quiz.explain: "Aiming for between noon and 4 p.m. is a good kind of range."

quiz.q: Who can extend a nap up to two hours?
choices: People who sleep a lot at night
People like a swimmer who must get up at 5 a.m.
quiz.explain: People who can't get enough sleep at night, like a swimmer up at 5 a.m., can nap up to two hours.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: So napping is super important.
It's important for athletes
and it's important for the general population.
If you're able to take
even a 15, 20-minute nap,
power nap has been shown
to increase levels of alertness, boost mood.
And even in those people
who are getting a good amount
of sleep at night,
the naps have been shown
to be even more beneficial for them as well
as far as with regard to productivity
and alertness, et cetera.
So napping is important.
We recommend about a 20-minute nap.
So you would set your alarm
for about 30 minutes.
And then, you know, if your alarm goes off,
if you wake up before your alarm,
certainly get up.
And then the timing of the nap
is important as well.
So we don't want to nap
too close to bedtime.
So aiming for between noon and 4 p.m.
is a good kind of range.
And then for those athletes
or for those people who may not be getting
enough sleep at night,
so for example,
a swimmer who has a 5 a.m.,
or, you know,
has to get up at 5 a.m.,
it's likely that they're not able
to get enough sleep at night.
So extending that nap
to no more than two hours
is important for them
to make up some of that
lost sleep at night.

lessons.speaker: Alan Flanagan
lessons.role: Nutrition researcher, co-host of Sigma Nutrition Radio
lessons.title: Morning Lark or Night Owl?
lessons.title_ja: 朝型？夜型？
lessons.episode: #579: Is Your Chronotype Hard-Wired or Modifiable? And What Does It Mean for Health?

vocab.ja: クロノタイプ（朝型・夜型のタイプ）
夜型の人（夜のふくろう）
好きなようにさせておくと

quiz.q: What does "chrono" mean?
quiz.explain: "Chrono, obviously time — time type, so to speak."

quiz.q: What is a "morning lark"?
choices: A bird that sings at night
quiz.explain: A morning lark is a morning or early chronotype.

quiz.q: What is a "night owl"?
quiz.explain: Night owls would be a late or an evening chronotype.

quiz.q: When does sleep-wake timing show your chronotype best?
choices: When you have a lot of work
When you have no time constraints
quiz.explain: It's a good proxy "if it's an individual without any time constraints."

quiz.q: What mostly drives the preference?
quiz.explain: It's an expression of an internal, largely genetically driven preference.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: So the term itself does provide
a degree of giveaway in chrono,
obviously time, time type, so to speak.
And this chronotype is essentially denoting
an individual's behavioral expression
of their sleep-wake timing preferences.
We would often colloquially refer to this concept
as a morning lark
for a kind of a morning chronotype
or an early chronotype,
as it would be referred to,
or night owls,
which would be a late or an evening chronotype.
And I use the word behavioral expression
quite particularly
because this is related to the period
of their internal biological time, so to speak.
So the sleep-wake cycle provides essentially a proxy,
particularly if it's an individual
without any time constraints.
So left to one's own devices,
what would their self-selected sleep-wake timing be?
So that sleep-wake timing is a behavioral expression,
but it's an expression of internal,
largely genetically driven preference
for time-of-day related behaviors.

lessons.speaker: Alan Flanagan
lessons.role: Nutrition researcher, co-host of Sigma Nutrition Radio
lessons.title: Outdoor Light Moves Your Clock
lessons.title_ja: 外の光が体内時計を早める
lessons.episode: #579: Is Your Chronotype Hard-Wired or Modifiable? And What Does It Mean for Health?

vocab.ja: 外の合図がない時の体内時計の周期
ツァイトゲーバー（体内時計を合わせる合図）

quiz.q: Without any environmental signals, how long would circadian rhythms run?
quiz.explain: They would run for a little over 24 hours, about 24.2 hours.

quiz.q: What does the German word "zeitgeber" mean?
quiz.explain: "The German word zeitgeber, literally time giver."

quiz.q: What happens with weak time cues like indoor lighting?
quiz.explain: Weak zeitgebers typically result in the internal clock drifting later rather than earlier.

quiz.q: How much does the clock advance per hour of outdoor light?
quiz.explain: The internal clock advances by an average of about 30 minutes per one hour of outdoor light exposure.

quiz.q: After you adapt to a new time zone, what happens to your chronotype?
quiz.explain: Your chronotype doesn't change; you remain an evening chronotype.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: And so, for example, we typically,
as humans, mammals, have a free-running period.
If there was no environmental signals,
circadian rhythms would run
for a little over 24 hours, about 24.2 hours.
And so if you have strong environmental signals,
like you are outdoors in natural light exposure
all day, for example,
you will typically see that
with that strong strength of that time cue,
which is known in the literature
by the German word zeitgeber,
literally time giver,
that will typically result in circadian rhythms
synchronizing in an earlier phase
to the 24-hour day.
Whereas if we have weak strength of zeitgebers,
which we typically do
in Western industrialized countries,
we have urban environments, indoor lighting,
artificial light exposure,
this typically results in the phase
of the internal clock drifting later
rather than earlier.
Whereas, like I said,
when the environment emits strong time cues
such as natural light conditions,
the internal clock advances
by an average of about 30 minutes
per one hour of outdoor light exposure.
Now, this is still chronotype dependent.
If you're a late chronotype,
that shifting forward is not you shifting
as forward as an early chronotype,
if that makes sense.
It's still chronotype dependent.
So if you fly from London to Sydney
and you are massively jet-lagged
for up to a week,
you don't, your chronotype doesn't change
when you have synchronized
and adapted to your new time zone.
You remain an evening chronotype, you remain.
But the strength of those time cues
can influence the phase, shall we say,
of the internal clock timing.

lessons.speaker: Alan Flanagan
lessons.role: Nutrition researcher, co-host of Sigma Nutrition Radio
lessons.title: Why Flying East Is Harder
lessons.title_ja: 東へ飛ぶ方がつらいわけ
lessons.episode: #579: Is Your Chronotype Hard-Wired or Modifiable? And What Does It Mean for Health?

vocab.ja: ずれている、合っていない

quiz.q: Which direction of travel tends to be easier?
quiz.explain: "Going west tends to be easier."

quiz.q: Flying from London to New York is like...
choices: Staying up later in the day
quiz.explain: It involves a delay — "it's essentially like staying up later in the day."

quiz.q: Why is flying east more challenging?
choices: The system has to advance, which is more difficult
quiz.explain: Advancing the system is more difficult because of the realignment that must occur.

quiz.q: What influences the peripheral clocks very much?
quiz.explain: Peripheral clocks are very much influenced by behavior such as meal timing.

quiz.q: On average, how fast does melatonin adjust to a new time zone?
quiz.explain: Melatonin on average adjusts by about one hour a day (one older study found about 1.3 hours).

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: Well, typically what we know,
because human free-running circadian rhythms
tend to drift later than the 24-hour day,
what that typically means
from a kind of transmeridian air travel perspective
is generally going,
and I'm sure most of our listeners
probably in their own subjective experience
can maybe relate to this,
going west tends to be easier.
Again, if you fly from London to New York
or Chicago,
that involves essentially a delay.
It's essentially like staying up later in the day.
That tends to be slightly easier on the system
and there is less pronounced jet lag
or it's easier for the system
to overcome that kind of delay.
Advancing the system tends to,
again, if you were flying east
from London to Hong Kong or London to Singapore
or London to Sydney,
that is more challenging on the system
because of the realignment that must occur.
It's more difficult to advance
in that kind of context.
What's really occurring with jet lag
is we've got the central circadian clock,
which is light-driven primarily,
and our peripheral clocks,
which are very much influenced by behavior
such as meal timing,
they're misaligned to these environmental time cues
in the new time zone.
Now, because we're in that new time zone
with the timing of these zeitgebers,
these cues in our new time zone,
we will gradually realign to that.
And that does depend on the direction of travel,
like I said, so whether it's east or west,
and of course the number of time zones crossed.
So the magnitude of adaptation
typically is rate limited by melatonin,
which on average adjusts
by about one hour a day
to the timing of a new light-dark cycle.
There is inter-individual variation in that.
There is some older jet lag research
where they flew people
from the east coast of America to the UK,
and they had an average adaptation
of about 1.3 hours per day.

lessons.speaker: Shona Halson
lessons.role: Senior Recovery Physiologist, Australian Institute of Sport
lessons.title: Ice Bath by the Numbers
lessons.title_ja: 冷水浴は10〜15度で10〜15分
lessons.episode: SNR #192: Shona Halson, PhD - Recovery Strategies for Elite Performance

vocab.ja: 冷水につかること（冷水浴）
水分を十分にとっておく

quiz.q: What does research suggest for cold water?
quiz.explain: Cold water is something like 10 to 15 degrees for 10 to 15 minutes.

quiz.q: If the water can't get very cold, what might athletes do?
choices: Stay in slightly warmer water for longer
quiz.explain: Have the athlete hop in water that's slightly warmer for longer periods of time.

quiz.q: What ratio do they use for contrast therapy?
choices: The same time for hot and cold
quiz.explain: They keep the ratio the same — two minutes hot, two minutes cold.

quiz.q: Why don't they want athletes in a hot spa for too long?
choices: It's hard to keep athletes hydrated
quiz.explain: It's hard to get athletes to remain hydrated, so they avoid overcooking the body.

quiz.q: What temperature is the spa in Canberra?
quiz.explain: "The temperatures that we use in Canberra are 38 degrees for our spa."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: Yeah, look, I guess now
over the last couple of years,
there's been quite a bit of research
in the area.
And if you look specifically at research first
rather than practice.
So research tends to be in terms of
the scientific evidence
that's shown benefits of these strategies.
So your cold water, for example,
is something like 10 to 15 degrees temperature
for 10 to 15 minutes.
Contrast water, there's been less research in that area,
but again, suggesting around about
that sort of 10 to 15-minute type approach.
When it comes to practice,
there's obviously lots of things
that are going to depend
on whether you can have that amount of time
in the water.
So some of the things
that we think about are,
you know, what's the schedule of the athlete?
You know, are they a footballer who's just played
and then they have to go
and have media commitments and travel commitments, etc.?
What is the size of the equipment
that you've got available?
If you've got a large number of athletes
to get through a fairly small facility,
then that obviously makes things difficult as well.
And then you also have, you know,
considerations around what's the water temperature.
So if you're out in the field
and you're trying to do these recovery strategies
or you're at a competition setting
and, you know, you may not be able
to get water temperatures very low,
so what you might do is have the athlete
hop in water that's slightly warmer
for longer periods of time.
But if you look at, you know,
if people are interested
in what's a generic kind of protocol,
you'd probably look at 10 to 15 minutes,
10 to 15 degrees for cold water.
We like to keep the ratio the same
for the hot to cold
when you're talking contrast therapy.
So, you know, one minute, one minute
or two minutes, two minutes.
So two minutes hot, two minutes cold,
two minutes hot, two minutes cold,
something like that.
And again, you probably don't need to go
more than about 15 minutes.
And the hot water,
the only thing
that we really take into consideration there
potentially is, you know,
we don't want people sitting
in a hot spa for too long.
Mainly in our experience, we find that,
you know, it's hard
to get athletes to remain hydrated
at the best of times.
So not overcooking the body
by staying in hot water too long.
So again, the sort of 10 to 15 minutes
in a spa is pretty good.
The temperatures that we use in Canberra
are 38 degrees for our spa.

lessons.speaker: Shona Halson
lessons.role: Senior Recovery Physiologist, Australian Institute of Sport
lessons.title: Belief Helps Recovery
lessons.title_ja: 信じている回復法は取り上げない
lessons.episode: SNR #192: Shona Halson, PhD - Recovery Strategies for Elite Performance

vocab.ja: 〜するよう人に無理強いする

quiz.q: How are athletes when they leave the recovery center?
quiz.explain: "They're very different individuals when they leave."

quiz.q: Which is NOT mentioned as part of the recovery center experience?
quiz.explain: She mentions being in water, a social environment, temperature changes, hydrostatic pressure and hanging out with mates.

quiz.q: Who usually doesn't come into the center?
quiz.explain: "The coach usually doesn't come in," so it's a relaxed environment.
