quiz.q: What does she do if an athlete has tried ice baths and really doesn't like them?
quiz.explain: She wouldn't force them; she'd find an alternative strategy that works for them.

quiz.q: What is "the last thing you want"?
choices: A stressed, unhappy athlete doing recovery every day
An athlete who likes ice baths
quiz.explain: "The last thing you want to do is have a stressed, unhappy athlete doing recovery every day."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: Yeah, most definitely.
We see this all the time
in the recovery center at the AIS.
You know, athletes come into the center
and obviously they've finished hard training
and they're very different individuals when they leave.
So there's something about being in water.
There's something about being a social environment,
whether it's temperature changes,
whether it's hydrostatic pressure,
whether it's hanging out with their mates.
The coach usually doesn't come in.
So it's usually quite a, you know,
a relaxed environment.
So if the athletes
kind of get used to this
and they feel that they get benefits from them,
whatever benefits they may think that is,
to take that away from them
when they believe in something
can be problematic.
But on the flip side of that is,
you know, we do have athletes
who really don't like doing ice baths.
And if I know that they've tried it,
I trust them.
I know they're not just complaining and being lazy.
I wouldn't force them to do it
if it's something that's really unpleasant for them.
It would be about, OK,
let's try and find an alternative recovery strategy
that you feel works for them,
because the last thing you want to do
is have a stressed, unhappy athlete
doing recovery every day
and thinks that either it harms them
or it doesn't work for them.
So as long as they've tried it
and they've experienced it,
then I think it's OK not to push them
to do strategies,
even though we might think
there's some good science for it.

lessons.speaker: Shona Halson
lessons.role: Senior Recovery Physiologist, Australian Institute of Sport
lessons.title: Just Ask How They Feel
lessons.title_ja: 一番の目安は「どう感じるか」
lessons.episode: SNR #192: Shona Halson, PhD - Recovery Strategies for Elite Performance

vocab.ja: 自分で感じたことの点数

quiz.q: Before making decisions, how long should you track the data?
quiz.explain: Track it for a relatively long time before you make decisions — which not a lot of coaches like.

quiz.q: Why give good, quick feedback to athletes and coaches?
choices: So they are more likely to do it, and do it honestly
quiz.explain: With feedback, they think it's worth doing, so they're more likely to do it honestly.

quiz.q: Which simple questions does she ask a team?
choices: How recovered do you feel? How fatigued are you?
quiz.explain: "How recovered do you feel? How fatigued are you?"

quiz.q: What was her PhD about?
quiz.explain: "My PhD was on overtraining," with studies in cyclists.

quiz.q: What was the best predictor of performance changes?
choices: Their subjective ratings of how they felt
quiz.explain: The best predictor was their subjective ratings of how they felt — the thing that costs no money to measure.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: So I think the key is the combination
of the external and the internal,
tracking it for a relatively long time
before you make decisions,
which not a lot of coaches like.
Also giving good, quick feedback
to the athletes and coaches
so that they're more likely to do it
and do it honestly
because they think it's worth doing
because they're getting some feedback on it.
So yes, it's not a simple thing to do,
but I think really if done well,
there's so much good information
that you can get back to the athlete
to change the way they're training
and to see if they're really recovering or not.
And if we're working with a team
where we start periodizing training,
we're asking them simple questions like,
how recovered do you feel?
How fatigued are you?
And seeing how that changes over time.
And just as a very quick side note,
my PhD was on overtraining
and we did a couple of studies in cyclists
and measured every single thing under the sun,
from stable isotope infusion to look at metabolism,
every hormone, every blood marker
that you could measure.
And the best predictor of their performance changes
was their subjective ratings of how they felt.
The thing that doesn't cost any money to measure.
So I think we shouldn't underestimate the value
of asking the athletes good questions.

lessons.speaker: Katherine Appleton
lessons.title: Sweet Likers and Sweet Dislikers
lessons.title_ja: 甘い物が好きな人、苦手な人
lessons.episode: #612: Does Sweet Taste Exposure Actually Develop Preference? – Prof. Katherine Appleton

vocab.ja: 逆U字（上がってから下がる形）

quiz.q: What happens to "sweet likers" when a drink gets sweeter?
quiz.explain: As the sweet taste concentration increases, their preference increases: "an upward trajectory."

quiz.q: What are people who like a drink less as it gets sweeter called?
quiz.explain: "These people are referred to as sweet dislikers."

quiz.q: What does an "inverted U shape" mean here?
choices: Liking goes up to a point, then drops
quiz.explain: "It peaks at a certain concentration and then beyond that it will drop."

quiz.q: What did people think about these types in the past?
choices: They are a stable characteristic of each person
quiz.explain: There is a suggestion that this is "very much a stable characteristic of individuals."

quiz.q: What does newer evidence suggest?
choices: It may depend more on the situation, and people may vary
quiz.explain: There's increasing evidence that it may be "a bit more context specific" and that people may vary.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: There is the suggestion in the literature certainly
that yes, some people,
as a sweet taste concentration increases,
their preference increases.
It's very much an upward trajectory.
Those people are referred to as sweet likers,
or in some cases extreme sweet,
or sweet extreme likers.
There are individuals as well
that go the other way.
So as the concentration of sweetness
in a solution or a product increases,
their liking for it decreases.
So essentially it's a downward trajectory.
These people are referred to as sweet dislikers.
And then there's a group in the middle
who potentially either their sweet liking
for a solution will remain the same
regardless of the concentration,
or their response looks more like
an inverted U shape.
So essentially it peaks at a certain concentration
and then beyond that it will drop.
There is the suggestion,
these are referred to as sweet liker phenotypes.
So there is a suggestion
that this is very much
a stable characteristic of individuals,
but there's increasing evidence to suggest
that this may not be
in actual fact the case.
That it may be a bit more context specific,
but also that people may vary
as a result of all types of characteristics.

lessons.speaker: Katherine Appleton
lessons.title: Vegetables Grow on You, Sweetness Doesn't
lessons.title_ja: 野菜の味は慣れる、甘さは慣れない
lessons.episode: #612: Does Sweet Taste Exposure Actually Develop Preference? – Prof. Katherine Appleton

vocab.ja: （くり返し）ふれること、慣れさせること

quiz.q: What question do both kinds of studies ask?
choices: Does tasting something often make you like it more
quiz.explain: Both ask whether exposure to a taste or flavor increases liking, preference or consumption.

quiz.q: What did studies find about sweet taste?
choices: More exposure makes people love sugar
There is no evidence that exposure changes liking
Sweet taste is bad for children
People get tired of sweet taste
quiz.explain: "In sweet taste we find no evidence that there's any association between exposure and liking or preference."

quiz.q: What can happen with vegetable flavors?
choices: Tasting them more can increase acceptance and consumption
quiz.explain: Exposure to a vegetable flavor may result in increased acceptance, preference and consumption.

quiz.q: Why might vegetables be different from sweetness?
choices: Sweet taste is very general, but vegetable work looks at specific flavors
quiz.explain: "Sweet taste is very generic," while the vegetable work looks specifically at individual flavors.

quiz.q: How long does the vegetable effect last?
choices: It fades after about six months to a year
quiz.explain: "Six months, a year later, these effects that researchers are finding have dissipated."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: A lot of the work
that we've been doing recently
has looked at sweet taste,
and essentially sweet taste
in a number of different food products,
or a number of different,
essentially a number of different eating scenarios.
Compared to that, there is work,
and we've been looking at, sorry,
does sweet taste exposure impact
on liking or preferences
for subsequent sweet taste
or sweet tasting food products?
Compared to that,
there is some work in the vegetable world
looking at essentially the same question.
Does exposure to a vegetable flavor
result in increased preferences or liking,
and increased acceptance or increased consumption
of that vegetable flavor?
Here, while in sweet taste
we find no evidence
that there's any association
between exposure and liking or preference,
in the vegetable world there is the suggestion
that exposure to a vegetable flavor or vegetable taste
will result in subsequent increased acceptance,
increased preference and increased consumption
of that vegetable flavor.
There's clearly here a difference between these two.
We think at the moment
that sweet taste is very generic.
It's a taste that's much broader,
whereas the work in vegetables
is looking specifically at individual flavors,
so the flavor of a vegetable,
which may be transferred
to other similar vegetable flavors,
a similar kind of bitter taste or flavor.
But, yeah, it's a slightly different scenario
to the sweet taste scenario,
which we are considering more broader.
Also, though, to mention,
seeing as you've mentioned the vegetable work,
some of these studies in vegetables
do demonstrate this effect of exposure,
but even there it doesn't last for very long.
It's kind of six months, a year later,
these effects that researchers are finding have dissipated.
Many of these studies are also done with children,
and there may be differences here as well.

lessons.speaker: Katherine Appleton
lessons.title: Why We Eat What We Eat
lessons.title_ja: 何を食べるかは、味だけで決まらない
lessons.episode: #612: Does Sweet Taste Exposure Actually Develop Preference? – Prof. Katherine Appleton

vocab.ja: 味・におい・食感などの性質

quiz.q: According to her, where does taste rank among reasons we eat a food?
choices: It is high up, one of the primary reasons
quiz.explain: Taste and sensory characteristics "are high up there," one of the primary reasons.

quiz.q: Besides taste, what else is a huge factor?
quiz.explain: "Pleasure and enjoyment is a huge factor as well."

quiz.q: Which is an example of people's attitudes toward a food?
choices: Whether they think it is healthy or might do them harm
How long it takes to cook
quiz.explain: People perceive a food in terms of "is it healthy, will it potentially do me harm?"

quiz.q: What does "environmental factors" refer to here?
choices: What foods you have available to you
quiz.explain: Environmental factors determine "what foods do you have available to you."

quiz.q: Whether people cut down on sugar depends partly on what?
choices: The alternatives they see, like sweeteners, fruit and dairy
quiz.explain: It depends on "the alternatives they see available to them," such as low calorie sweeteners, fruits and dairy products.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: There are a huge number of different factors
that can impact
whether somebody consumes a food or not.
This is something that's very interesting.
The work that we've spoken about so far
is really focused on preference or liking,
preference, sweet taste perception and so on.
But yes, of all the reasons
that we consume a food,
taste and sensitivity or sensory characteristics
are high up there.
They are one of the primary reasons
that people consume the foods that they do.
Pleasure and enjoyment is a huge factor as well,
you can imagine.
But there are a lot of other reasons
for people consuming the foods that they do,
many of them related to their cognitions
or their attitudes
or how they perceive a food in terms of,
is it healthy,
will it potentially do me harm?
There's obviously a lot of environmental factors as well
that will determine what the foods that you consume,
essentially what foods do you have available to you.
And then yes, not only
what foods do you have available,
but what foods do you have as an alternative.
And this is an interesting question
when we think about low calorie sweeteners as well,
to go back to sweet taste.
Because of course, whether people are willing
to reduce their sugar consumption
will depend on the alternatives
they see available to them.
And some of this will depend on not only
their attitudes towards sugar
or the foods, sugary foods that they have available,
but their attitudes to the alternatives.
So low calorie sweeteners,
but again, fruits, dairy products,
natural sources of sweetness.

lessons.speaker: Andrew Reynolds
lessons.role: Research Associate Professor, University of Otago
lessons.title: What Makes a Nutrient Essential?
lessons.title_ja: 「必須の栄養素」って何？
lessons.episode: #603: Should Dietary Fiber Be Considered Essential? – Andrew Reynolds, PhD

vocab.ja: 必須栄養素（体に欠かせない栄養素）
結局〜ということになる
条件、基準（criterion の複数形）

quiz.q: What surprised him when he went looking?
choices: Every country had the same list
No single organization had a clear definition or list
Fiber was already on the list
quiz.explain: He "didn't find a sole body that had the concrete definition of an essential nutrient."

quiz.q: Which is one of the conditions for an essential nutrient?
choices: The body cannot make enough of it by itself
quiz.explain: "The body couldn't produce enough of that product of itself," so it had to come from diet.

quiz.q: What example does he give of a deficiency state?
quiz.explain: "So vitamin C and scurvy." When the nutrient came back, the deficiency went away.

quiz.q: Why was it easier to find essential nutrients more than 50 years ago?
choices: Ethical concerns did not stop such trials, and long sea voyages showed deficiencies
quiz.explain: Ethical concerns weren't a problem then, and on long sea voyages people went without fruit and vegetables for months.

quiz.q: How many main criteria did they want to address?
quiz.explain: "Those were the three sort of main criteria that we wanted to address."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: And when I went looking,
I didn't find a sole body
that had the concrete definition
of an essential nutrient,
or a sole body or organization
that had a list of
these are the essential ones
and these are not the essential ones.
So that in itself was interesting.
All of the main sort of caveats
boiled down to
that the body needed the nutrient to survive.
So it had to have a physiological function
that was recognized.
The body couldn't produce enough of that product
of itself to service its own needs.
So it did have to come
from things like diet.
And then probably the more trickier one
is that there had to be a certified
or obvious deficiency state that could be reversed.
So if you removed the nutrient,
an illness occurred.
So vitamin C and scurvy.
And then when you returned the nutrient,
the deficiency state went away.
And that sort of framing
makes a lot of sense
for when most of the essential nutrients
were discovered more than 50 years ago,
where things like ethical concerns
and trials weren't a problem.
You could deprive people of nutrients
and see what happened.
Or there was natural situations
such as the long sea voyages
where people were without fruit and vegetables
for months and months,
where you'd naturally sort of observe
deficiency states popping in for micronutrients.
Those were the three sort of main criteria
that we wanted to address.

lessons.speaker: Andrew Reynolds
lessons.role: Research Associate Professor, University of Otago
lessons.title: Which Fiber Is Best?
lessons.title_ja: いちばん良い食物繊維はどれ？
lessons.episode: #603: Should Dietary Fiber Be Considered Essential? – Andrew Reynolds, PhD

vocab.ja: もともと含まれている

quiz.q: What does he say when people ask for the best type of fiber?
choices: He doesn't give a clear answer because he doesn't have one
He says fruit fiber is the only good one
He says to take a supplement
quiz.explain: "I don't give them a clear answer because I don't have a clear answer."

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three classes of fiber he mentions?
choices: Fiber that you drink as a gas
quiz.explain: The three classes are inherent, extracted, and synthetic.

quiz.q: What do studies show about the health benefits of these three classes?
quiz.explain: "We don't see a difference between those three classes."

quiz.q: Why is there "a small vote" for fiber that is found in food?
choices: With fruit, you also get vitamins and minerals
quiz.explain: "If you have fruit, you're not just having fiber, you're also having the vitamins and minerals."

quiz.q: What does he think about adding more fiber to foods in the food supply?
choices: It is not a bad thing at all
quiz.explain: "I don't think that's a bad thing at all."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: So when people ask me
what is the best type of fiber,
I don't give them a clear answer
because I don't have a clear answer.
You can look at fiber in many different ways.
One way to look at it
is inherent in the food,
so a fruit that has fibers in it,
extracted and added to food,
or synthetic made in a lab
and added to food.
At the moment, we don't say
there's a health difference between those three classes.
We don't see a clear difference
where inherent fibers are better for you
for a chosen disease
than an extracted or a synthetic.
So that really clears the way
for food formulation in our food supply
to have more fiber put into it.
I don't think that's a bad thing at all.
With inherent fiber,
obviously there's a nutrient bundling concept
where if you have fruit,
you're not just having fiber,
you're also having the vitamins and minerals,
and that wouldn't necessarily be fortified in the food.
So there's always a small vote for inherent fiber
that's found in food
above the extracted or synthetic.
But when you only look
at the benefits of that fiber,
we don't see a difference between those three classes.
A lot of people want a specific answer
of which fiber.
I'm working in the area myself
of, well, what are the fibers
or things considered fiber at the moment
that aren't doing function,
as opposed to which are the ones
that are definitely doing function.
You already said that fibers range
in different classifications or types.
So their viscosity, their solubility
and their action in the body is different.
That's fine.
I think we should have a range of those.

lessons.speaker: Andrew Reynolds
lessons.role: Research Associate Professor, University of Otago
lessons.title: Add Fiber Slowly
lessons.title_ja: 食物繊維はゆっくり増やす
lessons.episode: #603: Should Dietary Fiber Be Considered Essential? – Andrew Reynolds, PhD

vocab.ja: 全粒の（精製していない穀物）

quiz.q: According to him, what is the main issue with increasing fiber?
choices: It takes too long to cook
quiz.explain: "The main issue of increasing fiber intakes is when you do that too quickly."

quiz.q: How much fiber can half a can of beans have?
quiz.explain: Half a can of beans "can have up to 14 grams of fiber."

quiz.q: What happens to most people who add a lot of fiber suddenly?
quiz.explain: Most people will experience "some distress in terms of bloating and gas."

quiz.q: Which is one of his tips for eating more fiber?
choices: Eat beans at every meal from day one
Choose whole grain products over refined grains
quiz.explain: He suggests choosing whole grain products, eating vegetables with their skin, and more legumes, nuts and seeds.

quiz.q: What is his "only advice"?
choices: Increase fiber at a slower rate at first
quiz.explain: "Just do so at a slower rate initially. Don't go all in."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: The main issue of increasing fiber intakes
is when you do that too quickly.
So someone who's not used
to a high fiber diet
suddenly has half a can of beans,
which can have up to 14 grams of fiber.
They could double their intake with a bean salad.
They will experience,
most people will experience some distress
in terms of bloating and gas,
farting and stuff.
That is really just because
you've gone from a low intake
to a much higher intake really quickly.
And beans are the classic one.
If you talk to beans about most people,
legumes, they're so high in fiber
that people will say,
oh no, I always get gas and bloat.
It's really just that change in fiber intake.
So if you make a decision for yourself
to consciously increase fiber intakes,
if you start to choose those whole grain products
over refined grains,
and actively eat more vegetables
with their skin when appropriate,
and have more legumes, nuts and seeds,
just do so at a slower rate initially.
Don't go all in.
Don't suddenly triple your fiber intake,
because you will experience some distress
as that microbiome has to settle out
and start to flourish and control itself
with that sudden increase in food
that it can consume.
So that's my really only advice.
That's the only symptom I know,
or negative, about higher fiber intakes.
It's if you do it too quickly.

lessons.speaker: Luke Hanna
lessons.title: Eat More, Weigh Less: Volume Eating
lessons.title_ja: 量を減らさずにカロリーを減らす
lessons.episode: #606: Practical Nutrition Strategies for Fat Loss – Luke Hanna

vocab.ja: エネルギー密度（1グラムあたりのカロリー）
おなかを満たしておく
カロリー不足（使う量より少なく食べる状態）
だしやスープが中心の汁物
脂の少ないたんぱく質（鶏むね肉など）

quiz.q: What is "energy density"?
choices: The amount of energy in a particular weight of food
quiz.explain: It is "the amount of energy in a particular weight of food, normally expressed as calories per gram."

quiz.q: Why does he like volume eating?
choices: People don't feel like they are eating less, but they still eat fewer calories
quiz.explain: It makes them feel "like they're not eating less food overall," but puts them in a calorie deficit.

quiz.q: Which foods have a very low energy density?
choices: Fruit, non-starchy vegetables and broth-based soups
quiz.explain: Very low energy density (under 0.6 calories per gram) includes fruit, non-starchy vegetables and broth-based soups.

quiz.q: Which group do nuts belong to?
quiz.explain: High energy density (4 to 9 calories per gram) includes fried snacks, candy, cookies and nuts.

quiz.q: In his example, how many calories did the changes save in one meal?
quiz.explain: "You'd save around 170 calories just in that single meal," without eating less food.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: So there's something
that nowadays is being coined volume eating,
which has been popularized a lot through social media.
I really like this approach
for various different reasons,
but essentially what you're trying to do
is focusing on food that have low energy density,
energy density being the amount of energy
in a particular weight of food,
normally expressed as calories per gram.
So foods that have a low caloric content
but are voluminous
and take up a lot of space
on the plate,
trying to get them
to consume more of those foods
is going to help keep them full.
And I really like that strategy
because it can make them feel
like they're not eating less food overall,
but then it is putting them
in that calorie deficit,
which of course is required for long-term fat loss.
So from a technical perspective in research,
a very low energy density is something
that would be less than 0.6 calories per gram.
So that would be things like fruit,
non-starchy vegetables or broth-based soups.
A low energy density
is 0.6 to 1.5 calories per gram.
It'd be things like whole grains, lean proteins,
legumes and low-fat dairy.
Medium energy density would be 1.6 to 3.9.
So it's gonna be breads, desserts,
fat-free baked snacks, cheeses and higher fat meats.
Or high energy density,
which is gonna be
four to nine calories per gram.
And that's of course gonna be things
like fried snacks,
candy, cookies, nuts
and foods that tend to be fattier.
So trying to get people
to eat more of those
is a really nice way to do that
without making them feel like they're restricting
or having to eliminate anything.
And just to give like a practical example,
if I had a meal that was
100 grams chicken thighs,
100 grams pasta, 30 grams full fat cheese
and 100 grams mixed veg,
if I replaced the chicken thighs with chicken breast,
took 30 grams of the pasta
and added more vegetables, 30 grams more vegetables,
change the full fat cheese for low fat cheese,
you'd save around 170 calories
just in that single meal,
and you're not technically eating less food.
And so it's a really simple strategy
to make sure that they can
manipulate the energy balance
without feeling like they're doing so.

lessons.speaker: Luke Hanna
lessons.title: A Small Snack Before Dinner
lessons.title_ja: 夕食の前に、軽く一品
lessons.episode: #606: Practical Nutrition Strategies for Fat Loss – Luke Hanna

quiz.q: What is a "preload"?
choices: An intentional snack 15 to 30 minutes before a main meal
quiz.explain: A preload is "an intentional snack around 15 to 30 minutes before a main meal."

quiz.q: What kind of food is good for a preload?
quiz.explain: Things with low energy density, "like fruits or low calorie soups."

quiz.q: What did someone say about his social media video?
choices: "Are you talking about just having a starter?"
quiz.explain: Someone asked if he was "just having a starter." He said yes, but it's intentional.

quiz.q: Why do many people eat too much at dinner?
choices: They eat lunch at midday and are starving by dinner
quiz.explain: They might have lunch at midday, "and then by the time dinner rolls around, they're absolutely starving."

quiz.q: How does a preload help, according to him?
choices: It takes the edge off hunger so people make better decisions
quiz.explain: Something that "takes the physical edge off" makes it easier to make better decisions.

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: Similarly, another strategy,
actually also Barbara Rolls
has done a lot of research on,
is preloads,
which is essentially adding in an intentional snack
around 15 to 30 minutes before a main meal.
Things that are, again, low energy density,
so things like fruits or low calorie soups
and stuff like that.
It's quite funny.
Whenever I talk about this, I always think about
when I was talking about preloads
in one of my social media videos,
and someone was like,
are you talking about just having a starter?
And I was like, well, yeah,
but it's intentional,
and you're having a specific type of food.
But yeah, I think high volume
and or high fiber and protein,
salads, fruits and soups before a meal
can be quite effective.
And I think a lot of people as well
do struggle with portion control.
A lot of people
have sort of standard work days,
and they might have lunch at midday, one,
and then by the time dinner rolls around,
they're absolutely starving.
And then if they're making their meal at all,
rather than just ordering it,
it can be quite easy to start having
a little bit more than maybe they planned
with like pasta or portions of things like that,
and it can easily rack up.
But if you have something
that takes the physical edge off,
it can make it easier for people
to make better decisions.
And similarly,
even if you were going to order something,
I think that if you had something like that
before you made that decision,
you'd probably make a slightly better decision.

lessons.speaker: Luke Hanna
lessons.title: Put Down the Screen, Slow Down
lessons.title_ja: 「ながら食べ」をやめて、ゆっくり食べる
lessons.episode: #606: Practical Nutrition Strategies for Fat Loss – Luke Hanna

vocab.ja: おなかいっぱいのサイン

quiz.q: What is the first example of mindful eating he gives?
quiz.explain: "So for example, just eating without distraction."

quiz.q: What happens when people eat without distraction?
choices: They become more aware of hunger and fullness cues
quiz.explain: People are "more aware of their hunger and fullness cues, rather than just being in a sort of robotic state."

quiz.q: What did a 2015 meta-analysis find about chewing more?
choices: It may decrease hunger and food intake
It had no effect at all
quiz.explain: "Increased chewing may decrease self-reported hunger and food intake."

quiz.q: Which is a practical way to slow down?
choices: Put the cutlery down between bites
Drink a soda with the meal
quiz.explain: Things "like putting the cutlery down between bites, chewing more."

quiz.q: What did the 2013 study find about eating while distracted?
choices: It can affect how much you eat later in the day
quiz.explain: Eating distracted "can actually impact energy intake later in the day as well."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: There's sort of many different ways
that you can implement this.
There are a few ones
that crop up quite a lot.
So for example, just eating without distraction.
And we do have evidence to show
that if you are watching things while you eat,
and again, in today's society,
everyone's rushing and eating as fast as they can,
and not really thinking about what they're doing.
If you're eating without distraction, that can,
I think people are going to be
more aware of their hunger and fullness cues,
rather than just being
in a sort of robotic state,
which can help with portion control.
And then it can be slowing down as well.
As I say, so one systematic review,
a meta-analysis in 2015 found
that increased chewing may decrease
self-reported hunger and food intake.
So that could be quite beneficial.
And that could be practically be things
like putting the cutlery down between bites,
chewing more, that sort of thing.
But actually on the eating while distracted note,
there was actually a study
by Robinson et al in 2013
that found that eating distracted
can actually impact energy intake
later in the day as well,
which was quite interesting.
I don't think they quite understood why,
but yeah, it just shows how much
that can impact your overall dietary patterns.

lessons.speaker: Brendon Gurd
lessons.role: Professor of Exercise Physiology, Queen's University
lessons.title: Your Zone 2 Isn't Mine
lessons.title_ja: ゾーン2は人によって全然ちがう
lessons.episode: #571: Is Zone 2 Training Actually Best for Health? – Prof. Brendon Gurd

quiz.q: Why is it hard to know if you are in zone two?
choices: You need a heart rate watch
You need lab testing or lactate measurements to really know
Zone two is the same for everyone
quiz.explain: "It's actually really hard to know where your moderate intensity domain ends" without lab testing and measuring lactate.

quiz.q: What can zone two training be for a top cyclist like Tadej Pogačar?
quiz.explain: He said his zone two training intensity "can be 320 watts in some rides."

quiz.q: What can zone two be for recreationally active young adults?
quiz.explain: "Recreationally active young adults whose zone two lactate threshold would be like 60 watts."

quiz.q: What does he say about using a percent of max heart rate?
choices: It is probably not very accurate
It is the same as lab testing
quiz.explain: "Targeting a heart rate as a percent of max heart rate is probably not very accurate."

quiz.q: Why is "talking comfortably" not always a good test?
choices: Fit people cannot talk while exercising
A fit person's breathing can be high even in zone two
It only works in the lab
quiz.explain: "If you're a fit person with a really high lactate threshold, your ventilation is gonna be high even though you're still in zone two."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: Yeah, so I think it's actually really hard
to know where your moderate intensity domain ends.
So where the top of your zone two training
would be without doing lab testing
and measuring lactate.
Zone two can look really different
in different populations.
Elite athletes, I think Tadej Pogačar
was on a podcast,
said his zone two training intensity
can be 320 watts in some rides.
We have recreationally active young adults
whose zone two lactate threshold
would be like 60 watts.
So that's a huge difference.
So any sort of targeting a heart rate
as a percent of max heart rate
is probably not very accurate.
Ventilatory response, maybe you can kind of
use that idea of
if you're talking comfortably,
you might be in zone two.
But if you're a fit person
with a really high lactate threshold,
your ventilation is gonna be high
even though you're still in zone two.
So yeah, unfortunately, I think
if you really wanna know
am I in the moderate intensity domain,
you have to be either doing
a lot of lab testing
or measuring your lactate,
making sure lactate stays below two millimolar.

lessons.speaker: Brendon Gurd
lessons.role: Professor of Exercise Physiology, Queen's University
lessons.title: Why Athletes Go Easy
lessons.title_ja: 一流選手がゆっくり走る本当の理由
lessons.episode: #571: Is Zone 2 Training Actually Best for Health? – Prof. Brendon Gurd

vocab.ja: 持久系の選手（マラソン・自転車など）
グリコーゲン（筋肉にためた糖）
うっかり〜に入ってしまう
目安（ガイドライン）どおりの量

quiz.q: What does he say most people should do?
choices: Get above zone two as much as they can
quiz.explain: "We should actually be thinking about the opposite way as we want to get above zone two as much as we can."

quiz.q: Why do elite endurance athletes need recovery days?
choices: They do massive volumes of high intensity training
quiz.explain: "They're doing really high volumes of high intensity training and they need to have recovery days."

quiz.q: What happens if an athlete slips into zone three on a recovery day?
choices: They deplete glycogen, build up fatigue and stop recovering
quiz.explain: "If you slip up into that zone three and you start depleting glycogen, accumulating fatigue, now you're not recovering anymore."

quiz.q: Why does it make sense for athletes to stay in zone two?
choices: It is the best way to get fitter
They are trying to avoid stress so they can recover
It is the only zone they can do
quiz.explain: "It makes sense to me that you need to stay in zone two because you're trying to avoid stress."

quiz.q: Who probably doesn't need to worry about staying in zone two?
choices: People doing guideline levels of exercise
quiz.explain: "For most of us who are doing physical activity guideline levels of exercise, we probably don't need to worry about that."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: You want to go above zone two.
So I would guess where that idea comes from
is again, coming back
to those elite endurance athletes,
they're doing massive volumes of training.
They're doing really high volumes
of high intensity training
and they need to have recovery days.
They need to have days
where they're not stressing their system,
not accumulating metabolic stress.
And so in those athletes,
they want to stay below zone,
or in zone two, below zone three.
So they're not depleting glycogen,
not accumulating fatigue
so they can recover.
And I think if your aim is recovery,
if you slip up into that zone three
and you start depleting glycogen,
accumulating fatigue,
now you're not recovering anymore.
So in that setting, it makes sense to me
that you need to stay in zone two
because you're trying to avoid stress.
But for most of us
who are doing physical activity,
guideline levels of exercise,
we probably don't need to worry about that.
And I think we should actually be thinking
about the opposite way
as we want to get above zone two
as much as we can.

lessons.speaker: Brendon Gurd
lessons.role: Professor of Exercise Physiology, Queen's University
lessons.title: Your Zone 2 Might Be a Walk
lessons.title_ja: あなたのゾーン2は「歩く」かも
lessons.episode: #571: Is Zone 2 Training Actually Best for Health? – Prof. Brendon Gurd

vocab.ja: 運動する、トレーニングする
座っていることが多い、運動不足の

quiz.q: For many sedentary people starting to exercise, what is zone two?
quiz.explain: "Especially sedentary people who are starting to exercise, zone two would be walking."

quiz.q: What happens to him as soon as he starts jogging?
quiz.explain: "As soon as I'm jogging, I'm above zone two."

quiz.q: If you have 30 minutes but must stay in zone two, what does that mean for many people?
choices: A 30-minute walk instead of a 30-minute jog
quiz.explain: "That means you're just going for a 30-minute walk as opposed to doing a 30-minute jog."

quiz.q: Which gives more benefits, according to him?
quiz.explain: "There are benefits from walking for sure, but you're gonna get more if you jog."

quiz.q: What is zone two like for a marathon runner?
choices: The same as for the average person
quiz.explain: "For a marathon runner, zone two intensity is really fast, like they're running, but for the average person, it could be a walk."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: Yeah, I'm gonna come back
to the point you made
and this comes back to something
I talked about earlier
about how different zone two is
for different people.
And you know, like,
you're gonna go out and work out.
You wanna make sure
you're getting a good workout.
And for a lot of people, I think,
especially sedentary people
who are starting to exercise,
zone two would be walking.
And as soon as you start to jog,
that's probably true for me, I imagine,
as soon as I'm jogging, I'm above zone two.
So if you think about it in that context,
if we're actually telling people to go out
and you have 30 minutes to exercise,
but you need to be in zone two,
that means you're just going for a 30-minute walk
as opposed to doing a 30-minute jog.
And I think when you think about it
in that context, it's pretty intuitive that,
well, the benefits are gonna be better
from the jogging, right?
Not walking.
And there are benefits from walking for sure,
but you're gonna get more if you jog.
So I think that's an important context
in recognizing, like for a marathon runner,
zone two intensity is really fast.
like they're running,
but for the average person,
it could be a walk.

lessons.speaker: James Clear
lessons.title: The Decisive Moment
lessons.title_ja: その後の2時間を決める一瞬
lessons.episode: #249: Habits & Behaviour Change – James Clear

vocab.ja: 決定的な瞬間（その後を決める一瞬）
持ち帰りの料理（出前）を頼む
前もって決まっている

quiz.q: What happens at 5:15 PM in James's day?
choices: His wife comes home and they either change into workout clothes or sit on the couch
quiz.explain: "At 5:15 PM, my wife comes home from work and either we change into our workout clothes or we sit on the couch."

quiz.q: What determines what happens in the next two hours?
choices: The moment of changing into workout clothes
quiz.explain: "It's really the moment of changing into our workout clothes that determines what happens the next two hours."

quiz.q: What is his decisive moment in the morning?
choices: Opening Evernote to write, or going to ESPN for sports news
quiz.explain: "Either I open up Evernote and start working on the next article ... or I go to ESPN and check on the latest sports news."

quiz.q: How many decisive moments do most people have in a day?
quiz.explain: "For most people, there are maybe five or 10 decisive moments like that throughout the day."

quiz.q: What should you really focus on to change a habit?
choices: The first two minutes of the behavior
The last few minutes before bed
quiz.explain: "You're really focused on like the first two minutes of the behavior."

lines.en: And again, there are multiple ways
to approach this,
but I think one way that's very useful
is to focus on what I call
the decisive moment.
So for example, there are a couple
of decisive moments throughout my day.
Like at 5:15 PM,
my wife comes home from work
and either we change into our workout clothes
or we sit on the couch
and, you know, turn on reruns of The Office
or Netflix or something and order takeout.
And it's really the moment
of changing into our workout clothes
that determines what happens the next two hours.
If we do that one thing,
then we're gonna get in the car,
we'll drive to the gym,
we'll get under the bar,
we'll do the workout,
like the next two hours
are kind of already pre-decided if we change.
So it's really mastering the habit of working out
is really about mastering
that first little decisive moment.
And there's a similar moment in the morning
where I sit down
and either I open up Evernote
and start working on the next article
that I'm gonna write
or I go to ESPN
and check on the latest sports news or whatever.
And it's really about like
what I do in those first 60 seconds
that determines what the next like
40 minutes are gonna look like.
So I think for most people,
there are maybe five or 10 decisive moments
like that throughout the day,
little like forks in the road
that these inflection points
that determine how you're gonna spend
the next chunk of time.
And if you're trying to figure out
where should I focus first,
I would say focus on those decisive moments,
try to figure out like
what's the habit that I'm trying to change
and what is the decisive moment that precedes that,
that determines what that block of time
is gonna look like.
And what you come to realize
is that there isn't actually that much
that you need to change,
you're really focused on like
the first two minutes of the behavior.

lessons.speaker: James Clear
lessons.title: Master the Art of Showing Up
lessons.title_ja: まずは「行くだけ」を習慣に
lessons.episode: #249: Habits & Behaviour Change – James Clear

vocab.ja: よりよくする、最適化する
（どうせなら）〜したほうがいい

quiz.q: What mistake do people make even when they know they should start small?
choices: They still start too big, like running for 15 minutes
They run every day for an hour
quiz.explain: "Even when you know you should start small, it's still really easy to start too big."

quiz.q: What is the two-minute version of a running habit?
choices: Put on your running shoes and step out the door
quiz.explain: "The habit would be, I put on my running shoes and I step out the door."

quiz.q: Complete the sentence: "A habit must be ___ before it can be improved."
quiz.explain: "A habit must be established before it can be improved."

quiz.q: What rule did the reader follow at the gym?
choices: He had to stay for one hour
He couldn't stay for more than five minutes
He had to go with a friend
He could only use the treadmill
quiz.explain: "He went to the gym, but he wasn't allowed to stay for more than five minutes."

quiz.q: What happened after about six weeks?
choices: He stopped going to the gym
He decided to stay longer and do a better workout
quiz.explain: "I'm coming here all the time, I might as well start staying longer, doing a better workout."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: So, you know,
a lot of people have heard the idea
that they should start small or build small habits,
but even when you know you should start small,
it's still really easy to start too big.
So for example,
if you're trying to start a running habit,
then a lot of people say,
okay, I wanna run,
but I know that I should start small,
so let me just run for 15 minutes.
But even that is like way bigger
than what I'm talking about,
I'm talking about take your habit
and scale it down into the first two minutes.
So the habit would be,
I put on my running shoes
and I step out the door.
And if you do anything else more than that,
it's just a bonus.
If you go for a run,
it's just a bonus.
Now, some people will hear that and think that,
oh, this kind of sounds
like a gimmick or a trick,
like I know the real goal is to run,
I know it's not just
to put my shoes on.
But if you feel that way,
I would encourage you to do literally the opposite,
to stop after two minutes.
And the point of this entire exercise
is to get yourself
to master the art of showing up.
So the very first thing,
and this is the ultimate answer to your question
of what do you focus on first,
when you're building a new habit,
the very first thing you need to master
is the art of showing up.
A habit must be established
before it can be improved.
If you don't have a habit to begin with,
you don't have anything to optimize.
And so, as an example,
I had a reader
who he ended up losing a hundred pounds.
And one of the ways that he did it
was that he went to the gym,
but he wasn't allowed to stay
for more than five minutes.
He would show up, walk in,
maybe do an exercise,
and then once the clock hit five minutes
or his watch hit five minutes,
he would walk out the door.
And he did this for like six weeks.
And eventually he was like, you know,
I'm coming here all the time,
I might as well start staying longer,
doing a better workout or whatever.
And that sounds funny to people
when they first hear it,
but the point is
that he was mastering the art of showing up.

lessons.speaker: James Clear
lessons.title: Reward Good Habits Right Away
lessons.title_ja: いい習慣には「すぐのごほうび」を

quiz.q: What is the Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change?
choices: Behaviors that are immediately rewarded get repeated, and those immediately punished get avoided
You need 66 days to build a habit
quiz.explain: "Behaviors that are immediately rewarded get repeated and behaviors that are immediately punished get avoided."

quiz.q: What is the immediate outcome of eating a donut?
quiz.explain: "You eat a donut and right now it's tasty and sugary and enjoyable."

quiz.q: What is the immediate outcome of going to the gym?
choices: You get in shape right away
It's a little bit unfavorable: you sweat and breathe hard
You lose a lot of weight
quiz.explain: "The immediate outcome is a little bit unfavorable. You sweat, it takes sacrifice ... you're panting and breathing hard."

quiz.q: Why is going to the gym for one month not very rewarding?
choices: You don't see much change in your body or on the scale
quiz.explain: "You don't really see much of a change in your body ... The weight on the scale may not have changed that much."

quiz.q: Which is an example of an external reinforcement?
choices: Taking a bubble bath after going to the gym three days a week
quiz.explain: "If I go to the gym three days a week, every week that I do that, then I get to take a bubble bath."

lessons.credit: Clip: Sigma Nutrition Radio with Danny Lennon (sigmanutrition.com) — used with permission

lines.en: And in the book,
I explain a concept that I call
the Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change,
which is that behaviors
that are immediately rewarded get repeated
and behaviors that are immediately punished
get avoided.
So you can think of pretty much any behavior
as producing multiple outcomes across time.
So for example, a bad habit, the outcome,
the immediate outcome is often positive.
So for example, you eat a donut
and right now it's tasty and sugary and enjoyable.
But the ultimate outcome is unfavorable.
You gain weight in two weeks
or a month or whatever.
For good habits, it's often the reverse.
Going to the gym right now,
the immediate outcome is a little bit unfavorable.
You sweat, it takes sacrifice,
you have to work hard,
you're panting and breathing hard.
But the ultimate outcome is favorable.
You get in shape
in two weeks or a month.
And so much of the battle
of building good habits and breaking bad ones
is about taking the punishments of your bad habits
and finding a way
to move those into the immediate moment
and taking the rewards of your good habits,
the ultimate outcome,
and finding a way
to move that into the immediate moment.
And I think
when it comes to building good habits,
one of the best ways to do that
is to find an alternative way
to be satisfied in the moment
so that you're not waiting
for this long-term reward to show up.
You know, like the reward
for going to the gym for a month
isn't really a whole lot.
Like you don't really see
much of a change in your body.
People probably aren't commenting
on how you look different.
The weight on the scale
may not have changed that much.
So you need something more immediate
to feel satisfied.
And that can either be
with an external reinforcement,
like if I go to the gym
three days a week,
every week that I do that,
then I get to take a bubble bath
or I take a walk in the woods
or I get to watch my favorite TV show
for an extra hour or something like that.
